speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Minister of Transport) moved
speechtext:
that Bill C-44, an Act to amend the Western Grain Transportation Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Transport.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased today to rise and speak on second reading of Bill C-44 which was introduced in the House on April 26 last. I presume by now that all Members will have had a chance to look at the Bill and will recognize that it is a Bill that, among other things, covers a number of housekeeping items, but in addition contains some very positive and constructive provisions.
Bill C-44 contains amendments to the Western Grain Transportation Act. During the previous debate which took place in this Chamber in 1983 and 1984, it became clear that there were a number of deficiencies in the Act and a number of amendments, amendments which should have been considered and incorporated at that time but were not. It is with that in mind that we are presenting this Bill.
Further, during the course of the application of this Bill, the experience has brought about a number of other deficiencies such as the propensity for the very wide and erratic fluctuations in the producers' freight rate and the fact that certain producers are excluded from being represented on the Senior Grain Transportation Committee. In recognition of this, our Party while in Opposition identified a number of these issues and made a number of commitments to correct these deficiencies, and to introduce a number of improvements into the Act

June 20, 1985
Western Grain Transportation Act
which will provide a better, more simplified and stable system for the producers of grain in western Canada.
In our Party's western caucus meeting in Prince Albert last July the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) stated and I quote:
Any legislation affecting western grain transportation must be designed to work for producers... A Progressive Conservative Government will make the amendments to the Western Grain Transportation Act required to guarantee a growing and confident agricultural sector in western Canada.

Bill C-44, in conjunction with other initiatives undertaken by this Government, represents a fulfilment of that undertaking. In the Prince Albert declaration, we outlined our policy with respect to grain transportation, and I would like to take a few moments to review those commitments and our actions as a Government.
In Prince Albert, we made a commitment to freeze the existing freight rates paid by producers from any further increase pending the results of the legislative review of the Western Grain Transportation Act as it applies to the producers' ability to pay. Bill C-44 contains a ceiling provision ensuring that for the next two crop years, the crop years of 1985-86 and 1986-87, producers' freight rates cannot rise above the existing level, which is on average $7.70 per tonne. The amendment does allow for the rate to drop, and I am pleased to note that the CTC has indicated that on average, producers will be paying $6 per tonne to ship their grain in crop year 1985-86.
Second, we made a commitment to remove the 31.5 million tonne volume cap contained in the legislation which acts as a disincentive to increased production and exports. The volume cap provision in the Western Grain Transportation Act has been strongly criticized by most of the major farm groups in western Canada. The proposal to remove the cap contained in Bill C-44 was developed in western Canada by the Grain Transportation Administration and has been endorsed by the Senior Grain Transportation Committee, which represents a cross-section of the entire grain industry, including the producer groups and representatives of the elevator companies. We believe that given this broad support and the clear benefits of the tally system which we are proposing and have agreed to implement in the system will address the basic problems caused by the 31.5 million tonne volume cap which exists in the current legislation.
Third, we committed ourselves to imposing a moratorium on branch line abandonment and to stop any tampering with the physical aspects of any line until the legislative review is completed and all other options and innovations for continued branch line use explored. The moratorium is in place. In December, there was a request of Commissioner McDonough of the western CTC to undertake an examination of alternatives for branch lines affected by abandonment and Commissioner McDonough is due to report by June 30. I look forward to his recommendations.
Fourth, we made a commitment to immediately examine ways and means to provide improved services and equitable
rates for grain producers who are discriminated against geographically. I am pleased to inform the House that we are currently negotiating with the British Columbia Railway an agreement whereby producers in the Peace River block will benefit from the Western Grain Transportation Act. Given the importance of transportation links with the West Coast and the new Pacific Rim markets, this agreement will help develop the agricultural potential of the Peace River area. As well, the Commission under Commissioner McDonough is mandated to bring forth recommendations with respect to grain transportation services in this area and other frontier areas as well.
Fifth, we promised to include in the Western Grain Transportation Act the federal Government's commitment to branch line rehabilitation. Bill C-44 will ensure the provision of a branch line rehabilitation program funded by the Government of Canada until at least March 1990.
Sixth, we made a commitment to ensure that the railways will be much more accountable to grain producers and that they will hold annual accountability meetings with producers. Bill C-44 requires that the railways publish an annual statement of grain investment plans and will require the railways to hold annual producer meetings in all western provinces similar to those which have been held by the CNR this year and similar in nature to the accountability meetings that are held by the Canadian Wheat Board on a regular basis.
Seventh, we made a commitment to protect all the specialty crops under the Western Grain Transportation Act from railway demurrage charges. I am happy to report that no demurrage is currently being levied by the railways in this area.
Eighth, we made a commitment to remove the distortion in freight rates applying to grain and oilseeds and the processed versions of these products consistent with maintaining equal opportunities for economic development in all regions of Canada. In connection with this, the process which has been established has been done so by events over which we have had very little control.
The Hall inquiry, which was created as a result of the legislation, has completed its findings and issued a report. The Hall Report was tabled in the House on April 30. We are currently engaged in discussions with producer groups and all representatives of the grain transportation, production and handling industry. We are looking forward to the reaction to that report. The Government will have more to say on that issue in the next few weeks when the review process is established. The recommendations of the Hall inquiry are included as part and parcel of that total review.
Ninth, we made a commitment to examine ways and means to improve access to, and utilization of, producer cars which producers in all parts of Canadian Wheat Board designated areas considered to be an important and very basic right. My colleague, the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer), is currently consulting with those involved to ensure that the producer's ability to order his own
June 20, 1985

car is maintained. Producer cars remain an important and vital element of the grain transportation system.
These commitments represent a comprehensive grain transportation policy. We have acted promptly to turn the commitments into action. Both the Prince Albert statement and Bill C-44 are based on considerable consultation and discussion with producers and their organizations. We have listened to their concerns and we have acted to address the problems which they have identified. We have acted in such a way that, we believe, is consistent with their desires. I am pleased to note that the contents of Bill C-44 have been well-supported generally and endorsed by producers, producer groups and all those engaged in the production and handling of the transportation of grain.
Essentially, Bill C-44 can be divided into three groups: first, the clauses dealing with the freight rate ceiling, second, the clauses which put in place the tally adjustment proposal and remove the volume cap and third, the clauses which provide a greater voice for individual producers and increased railway accountability.
With respect to the freight rate ceiling, we believe that this amendment will provide an important degree of certainty for producers in planning for the next two crop years. During the past several years, producers have been severely affected by unstable prices, rising input costs and high interest rates. Added to that burden has been a rapidly increasing freight rate that has gone from an average of $4.85 per tonne on August 1, 1983, to $7.70 today. That represents an increase of 58 per cent in less than two years.
We recognize that no one action alone will cure all the problems which face our agricultural sector. However, we believe that measures like the ceiling, combined with other initiatives such as the fuel tax rebate, the Western Grain Stabilization pay-out, the reduction in interest rates, the red meat stabilization plan, the moratorium on Farm Credit Corporation foreclosures, the capital gains initiative which is in the Budget and relief from high interest rates for those farmers who were locked into severely high interest rates under the provisions of the FCC, should help to break the spiral of rising costs and thereby improve the financial health of the farm community. That is the goal of our agricultural policy. I am pleased to bring in this Bill which will complement and reinforce the actions which have been taken heretofore.
These initiatives will go a long way to help restore a healthy and vibrant agricultural environment. I would indicate that if the ceiling provision is triggered, the savings experienced by producers will be absorbed by the railways. We believe this should encourage the railways to be more sensitive in controlling their costs so that any rate increase will remain below the ceiling.
To provide further stability and certainty to the western farmer, we are going to institute a tally adjustment system and remove the 31.5 million tonne volume cap. One of the principal benefits of the tally system will be to eliminate the wild year to
Western Grain Transportation Act
year fluctuations in the producer's share of the freight rate which were caused in party by the volume cap. Also eliminated will be the complex interim and final adjustment provisions which have been severely critized both inside and outside the House.
The result will be a simplified rate setting mechanism generating fair, stable rates. The producer rate will be more closely related to the actual costs incurred when his grain is shipped than it is at present, thus providing the producer with a more accurate and predictable picture of his total cost. Under the current system, rates in the future could fluctuate by $5 per tonne year over year. This kind of instability could lead to distortions in shipping patterns, which makes planning more difficult for producers and shields any true sense of the costs involved.
The tally system is quite straightforward and simple. Any amount of the Government's commitment, which is essentially the Crow benefit plus its share of inflation costs, not utilized in one crop year will be carried forward as a credit for producers. Any over-payment by Government will be set off against this credit. It is anticipated that over and under-payments will tend to balance out, leaving no significant outstanding credit remaining over the long term.
There is a $150 million limit which will act as a protection device, ensuring that no excessive balance remains in the tally. In farming, as in any business, it is important to know your costs and the tally system will give producers the stability they need to plan for the years ahead. The Senior Grain Transportation Committee recognized the value of this proposal and I hope all Hon. Members will agree that it represents a significant improvement over that contained in the current legislation.
Bill C-44 also contains a number of changes to the Western Grain Transportation Act to strengthen the role of producers in shaping the grain transportation system. Producer representation on the Senior Grain Transportation Committee will be increased from four to eight. Alberta will now have two, Saskatchewan will have three, Manitoba will have two, and for the first time British Columbia will have a representative. As promised last November, B.C. producers will have the right to choose their representative, which will take place after this legislation is passed. As a further change to the Senior Grain Transportation Committee, we are making the specialty crops representative a full voting member instead of just an observer in recognition of the growing importance of these products to western agriculture. Under the current legislation, that representative sits on the Senior Grain Transportation Committee as an observer only and does not have voting rights. This will be changed in this legislation and that representative will be a full voting member.
Bill C-44 will also require the railways to publish their annual statement of grain investment plans which now goes only to the Minister, the CTC, the grain transportation administrator and the Senior Grain Transportation Committee. We believe it is important that the railways demonstrate publicly their commitment to grain transportation in return for

June 20, 1985
Western Grain Transportation Act
the substantial benefits they have received under the Western Grain Transportation Act.
As I said earlier, to further enhance their accountability, we will require the railways to hold meetings with the producers in each western province every year in order to discuss grain transportation issues. We think this will not only provide an opportunity for producers and railways to iron out some difficulties, but as well it will probably be most productive in giving the railways an opportunity to put forward what they see as their future plans regarding technological change and improvements in the system, and perhaps get a better spirit of co-operation in the grain production, handling and transportation system as a whole.
This is much more than just a public relations exercise. Both producers and the railways, we believe, need a better understanding of each others problems and opportunities if we are going to have a transportation system which best serves our farmers. The railways are doing this already with some degree of success, and I think that the encouragement in this legislation will make it a process which will be expected and which will be productive.
In a nutshell, Mr. Speaker, these are the amendments we are bringing forward. Bill C-44 does not pretend to address every issue. It deals with a number of specific and pressing matters which we felt needed immediate action. As well, the initiatives which are contained in this Bill fulfil a commitment which was made during the course of the election campaign and prior to it. There are many other issues surrounding the Western Grain Transportation Act. We believe these can most appropriately be dealt with during the comprehensive legislative review. I can assure Hon. Members that all aspects of the Act will be included in that review.
We believe that these amendments are positive. We believe they will improve the legislation and provide a better system for producers. We believe they are non-controversial and reflect representations made by farm organizations in western Canada. We believe that these amendments deserve the support and speedy passage by this House. We have the opportunity now to make these changes in time to benefit the producers during the 1985-1986 crop year. I urge all Members of the House to keep that in mind during the course of our future deliberations on this measure.
This is not an end, Mr. Speaker. I am sure that over time more changes to the Western Grain Transportation Act will be required. However, I believe it is a start in improving the Act and I hope that the House will support that objective.

Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to have an opportunity to say a few words on behalf of my Party with respect to Bill C-44, an Act to amend the Western Grain Transportation Act. I believe the most interesting thing about this Bill is that the Minister had a lot of concerns and hesitations in supporting the Western Grain Transportation legislation when it was brought into the House a couple of
years ago. However, we see in the legislation before us today only two substantive amendments and a number of housekeeping amendments to the Bill. Clearly the Minister must have been very supportive at the time the legislation was brought into the House.
As I recall, the Minister had some 14 objections to the legislation which was originally introduced in the House and now it seems that most of those objections have totally vanished, at least to the point where the Minister is concerned about bringing in amendments to the legislation. For instance, he was very concerned about the distortion between raw grain transportation prices as well as processed products. He was very concerned about increases in the transportation costs to the agricultural community. In fact, the initial price of grain has been reduced.
The Minister was also very concerned about distortions in the diversification of the western economy, yet there seems to be nothing in the Bill with respect to that. He felt the original Bill was far too generous to the railways and yet there is no action with respect to that. He was concerned about the erosion of the powers of the Canadian Wheat Board, yet there is no action in the Bill relating to that. I think we have a Bill here about which either the Minister has changed his mind or he is not concerned enough about to propose any more than two substantive amendments.
The press release issued by the Minister when the Bill received first reading said that the amendments would help western producers this coming year and give them more certainty in planning future crops. I would be interested to know exactly how this Bill provides additional help to western farmers in the 1985-86 crop year. The Minister has talked about the commitments of the Prince Albert declaration. He has talked about the actions which the Government is taking in agriculture. Any farmer in the red meat or grains industry will tell you that there has never been such a desperate situation with regard to commodity pricing. The Government has allowed 17 million pounds of subsidized European beef to come into the country.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) went to the United Kingdom saying that he would have great relations with the United Kingdom and solve all the problems. That is the problem with the Prime Minister. He is trying to solve every problem himself rather than giving some of that responsibility to his Minister. He is clearly making a bollix of it. At least,
1,000	carcases of subsidized beef are coming into Canada each week. There is a countervail on our hogs.
When the Minister talked about solving problems for the Canadian agricultural industry, he certainly was not referring to the red meat industry. When the President of the United States returned home after the Quebec summit, he imposed a countervail on hogs and unilaterally established a bonus program of $2 billion from reserves of grain to subsidize their wheat sales. That will have a devastating impact on western agriculture. It will reduce the price of grain by 10 to 15 per
June 20, 1985

cent, all of that in spite of the great song and dance team in Quebec City.
1 will not take the time of the House to recite all the other promises in the Prince Albert declaration which the Government has broken. However, it has reimposed 9 cents a gallon on farm fuel. In Western Canada that is called the "harvest tax" because it goes into effect on September 1. The Government broke its promise on agri-bonds. It is imposing a 1 per cent sales tax. The Minister talked about action in the farm debt crisis, but there has been no action in that area in the Budget or the Estimates of the Department.
Perhaps one of the worst breaches of promise by the Prime Minister was his failure to freeze freight rates at the 1983-84 levels. This Bill freezes them at the 1984-85 levels which are at least 20 per cent higher than those of 1983-84. Three days before the Bill was tabled in the House, the Canadian Transport Commission reported the rate scale for the upcoming year. The new rates for 1985-86 are in fact 22 per cent lower than the rates for 1984-85.
The Minister rushed the Bill into the House for first reading on April 26 because he knew that if he did not he would look very silly after April 29 guaranteeing that the rates would not exceed a level 22 per cent higher than what they already were. If this Bill had frozen rates at the 1983-84 levels or the 1985-86 levels, it would mean something. By choosing the 1984-85 rates, the high point in the cycle, the Minister is giving nothing to western farmers. His freeze is meaningless. The Minister is trying to take credit for a rate reduction which occurred naturally in any event.
The gift for which the Minister is trying to take credit is more or less like giving away the sleeves of his vest. With the reduced volumes, the rates in the crop year 1986-87 are not likely to exceed the levels which he froze them at last year. In Prince Albert last July, the Prime Minister made the very serious promise that he would freeze the rates at the 1983-84 levels rather than at the higher 1984-85 levels. Western farmers are very aware of that commitment and feel the Government should have carried through on it.
The Minister spoke about removing the volume cap. I feel that the amendments proposed in this Bill are commendable, but they do not really remove the volume cap. They simply create a new system for setting rates where the increases in volume over the cap in one year are set against years when the cap is not reached. It is assumed that over time these years will even out so that the producer will pay the same amount, but will not see the large fluctuations in rates which have occurred in the last two years. Unfortunately, while the new tally adjustment is fair for the system as a whole, it is not fair to individual producers whose year-to-year shipments do not necessarily reflect the over-all swings in the system. For example, a farmer who pays a higher rate than he should in one year is not necessarily the same farmer who will benefit from a lower rate the next year.
We support the changes scheduled for the Senior Grain Transportation Committee. We are in favour of seeing the
Western Grain Transportation Act representation increased. We would be interested to know why there have been no elections to fill the existing positions.
The branch line abandonment agreements have been signed with the railways, completing the promised program. The full commitment has been kept. It is the present Minister who has cut back the work to be done this year and moved the whole program back. Perhaps it is a good thing to put the commitment in the Act. It will save future cuts by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) or the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen).
We are all aware of what the Deputy Prime Minister is doing in that regard. He chooses a couple of bankers from Toronto or Montreal who study the Estimates of the department under consideration and make massive cuts. Each year for the next five years, $50 million will be cut from the Department of Agriculture. That will have a devastating impact on that department. We do not know exactly where the cuts will be made, but there is clearly a commitment in the Budget to cut the expenditures of the Department of Agriculture. I would like to know if any of those cuts will apply to western grain producers. I am sure the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) has access to that information. It would be very useful if he would provide that to the House this afternoon because from reading the budget documents, it is not clear where those cuts will occur. There is great apprehension.
Yesterday, the Ontario Federation of Agriculture met to plan action in response to the Government's lack of action in its Budget and the increase in farm input costs as a result of increased sales tax and excise tax on fuel.
The Minister mentioned the Hall committee report which came out in April. He has had ample time to consider its recommendations. He certainly objected to the current method of payments when the Bill was originally introduced and favoured a freedom of choice with regard to the Crow benefit payment. However, he never clearly identified what that freedom of choice position meant.
Many of his caucus colleagues were opposed to railway payments. That was one reason for the establishment of the Hall commission. Although it has reported, the Minister, to my understanding, has not yet indicated his preferred method for making that Crow benefit payment. The Minister of State for Transport (Mr. Bouchard), has taken a clear stand. He supports the UPA position in Quebec. Many of his caucus colleagues from Alberta favour a direct payment.
We would like to know if the Minister's position with regard to the Hall committee is to pay the railroads, pay the grain producers or a combination of those? Clearly, while this legislation makes a few substantive amendments, it does not deal with the 14 main objections made by the Minister when the original Western Grain Transportation Act was passed. Some of the objections he made at the time were the reduction of the power of the Wheat Board, the distortion in pricing between raw grain and processed products, the increased cost

When this Bill goes to the Standing Committee, I hope he will be able to clarify his position on those more substantial issues. While we agree with a freeze on transportation rates, the campaign commitment was to freeze them at the 1983-84 level, not at the higher level as the Minister has done.
Essentially he is giving away nothing. It will not only have a zero impact in the coming year, it will have a zero impact in the following crop year. Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on this Bill with some mixed feelings. The Minister will know from the bitter times of 1982-1983 and part of 1984 why my feelings are somewhat mixed. Of course, one definition of mixed feelings is watching one's monther-in-law go over a cliff in one's new car.
The system for sharing the cost of transportation of grain and other agricultural commodities in Canada, particularly from western Canada, has been in place in one form or another since the 1890s. Governments and Canadians since that time have recognized that because of our geography and the distance which we must move our commodities to reach export positions, as well as the activities of our competitors, that grain producers should not be called upon to pay the entire cost of transporting grain to export positions. As a nation we agreed to share the cost of moving that grain because its export benefits the country to the tune of some $4 billion or $5 billion a year in foreign exchange.
The activities of our competitors placed our grain producers in an awkward situation on a number of occasions. Furthermore, Argentina, one of our competitors, produces most of its grain within 200 miles of salt water-certainly not more than 500 miles. As well, the Government of Argentina has been moving that grain to export positions at no cost to the grain producers. Australia produces most of its grain within 200
miles of salt water. However, our average haul of grain to export positions is approximately 1,000 miles.
The United States has access to a massive inland water system, which is the cheapest way to move heavy bulk commodities like grain, and it was heavily subsidized and built at the taxpayers' expense because the U.S. corps of army engineers built it. Moreover, the United States subsidizes its grain producers by an amount of $8 to $12 a tonne. The European Economic Community has subsidies between $20 and $24 a tonne. We cannot expect our grain producers of western Canada to compete against the treasuries of those competing nations and organizations.
Those of us who live in the West want to ensure that the rest of Canada understands that situation as well as the fact that public funds being invested for capital improvements in the railway system not only helps to move grain but all commodities. Presently, grain only represents approximately 15 per cent to 20 per cent of the track capacity through British Columbia, while the remainder is taken up with other commodities. Therefore, this is not only a benefit to grain producers.
When the previous Government set out to destroy the Crow rate, it was our position that the railroad claims for losses were excessive, and that the Government should receive an equivalent value of equity ownership for any money given by the Government of Canada to the railroads for capital improvements. In other words, if $300 million goes to CN, the Government's equity ownership in shares in CN is automatically increased by that amount. On any funds going to Canadian Pacific, the Government of Canada should get common voting stock of an equivalent value. It seems to us that public investment, investment by taxpayers, is just as much entitled to a return on the investment as any private investor.
Why do we as a nation continue to hand the railroads money and get no return on it? That is a good sound private enterprise principle to which I am trying to educate my colleagues in the Liberal and Conservative Parties. If you are going to give Canadian Pacific money, take common equity voting shares in return and when a dividend is paid, the taxpayers will get something back on their investment. Taxpayers are just as much entitled as a private investor to an opportunity for a return on an investment. We will keep trying to persuade the Minister and the Government to act in that manner, which is an even more responsible use of public funds.
The Minister spoke about the rate freeze. I urge him to correct his Bill to state that the rate established for the 1985-86 crop year shall be the maximum rate for the ensuing two crop years. He himself was talking about freezing the rates at the 1984-85 level of $7.70 a tonne, yet in the next breath the Minister said that was something like a 53 per cent, 55 per cent or whatever figure increase in costs for western grain producers. He sounded to me that he thought that was too high an increase. I certainly agree with that. Why not have the Bill say that the rate that comes into effect for the coming 1985-86 crop year shall be the maximum rate for the ensuing
June 20, 1985

two crop years? Then you would have a genuine three year rate freeze.
I want to say to the Minister that we have had discussions, but I want to remind him about the situation in Prince Rupert. First, he mentions that there is no demurrage being charged on railway cars for specialty crops. When the committee was in Prince Rupert a while back, we were informed by employees who work around those terminals that some of the shippers and receivers are using those railway cars as storage. They let them pile up, back up. There are loaded cars sitting for weeks and months at a time waiting for a ship to come in. That is a very bad misuse of our railway cars. I would urge the Minister to take a second look at that matter. Perhaps he could check into whether there is an abuse. He has the power to make the shippers and receivers pay demurrage on those excessive delays to those kinds of shipments.
Second, when the committee held hearings in Vancouver and Prince Rupert, we were urged to make use of the old grain terminal at Prince Rupert. We were told that it should not be closed down but used for specialty crops and for surge capacity and cleaning and drying facilities. That terminal is still a good terminal. The federal Government a number of years ago put quite a few million dollars into upgrading it. It needs to be kept in place. If the consortium, the Prince Rupert Grain Company, does not want to operate it, then the Minister should.
I have come to the point about the argument concerning moneys provided under the Western Grain Transportation Act being paid to the railroad or whether that should be paid directly to the producers. We oppose the payments directly to producers for a number of reasons. We are not alone in our opposition. The three Prairie pools oppose it. The Saskatchewan Association of Rural Municipalities opposes it, the Saskatchewan Cow-Calf Operators opposes it and the National Farmers Union opposes it.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) and myself had an opportunity to meet with officers of UPA in Quebec last week. I suppose that is probably the largest farm organization in the country. The UPA adamantly opposes any direct payments to producers. I hope that is sufficient to persuade the Minister that he will not mess around with those payments, that he will continue to pay the railways and that he will finally agree to take equity ownership for any money given the railroads for capital investment.
The Minister in the Bill is increasing the number of representatives on the Senior Grain Transportation Committee by adding a representative from the Peace River district. We agree with that. We feel that if the Government is going to be expanding the membership of the committee, and here I am making a pitch for my own province, that that committee should adequately represent the Province of Saskatchewan. Why should the producers of 50 per cent or more of all the grain in western Canada not be represented 50 per cent? We would like to see the Minister increase the number in the Bill from eight to 10, so the Bill would read one representative from the Peace River country, two representatives each from
Western Grain Transportation Act Manitoba and Alberta and five from Saskatchewan. That would be a fair producer representation based to some degree on numbers, certainly based on Saskatchewan production, which is more than both Alberta and Manitoba put together.
The Minister is expanding the membership and moving the representatives for the non-permit bookholders, that will be the producers of specialty crops and so forth, to actual voting membership status rather than observer status. We agree with that. Again, the Minister will recall that when we were debating the original Bill, he and I succeeded in getting that observer status. We also succeeded in getting a representative on the committee from the trade union movement involved in the grain transportation business and grain handling.
I am asking the Minister if he would be willing to do it himself or accept an amendment that moves labour representative from observer status to full status. We think it would be proper to have two representatives from the labour movement, one from part of the labour movement involved in the transportation of grain, namely the railroad workers, and one representative from those who handle the grain, the grain handlers, longshoremen and so forth. We should have a representative from each of those categories. I would like the Minister to consider that, but we can talk about it some more in the committee. We think the committee could have representatives from other fields.
We have representatives from the producers, the elevators, the shippers, the haulers, the bureaucrats, the shipping companies and the truckers. Why can we not have representatives from the labour movement, as well as representatives from the port and harbour commissions involved in grain movement? I think they should also be on that committee. Should there not be a representative from Prince Rupert, one from Vancouver and one from Thunder Bay on the committee? There is also the St. Lawrence Seaway to consider. At least its representatives should be there as observers.
Grain producers have been waiting two years since the Bill became law. Farmers and all other people involved in the industry are waiting to get on with shaping the future of grain transportation. While we want the Peace River district and non-permit book holders to be voting representatives and to give advice to the Minister and the administrators, we also want to get on with the business of the committee. The Minister could put the committee to work and put these amendments entrain at the same time.
Section 62 of the Act provides for a full-scale review of all effects of the original Bill brought in by the Liberals to kill the Crow so that, as Hall said, the review could be done two years later. This would be after the committee had been fully constituted, had completed its collection of data, and had made small technical and regulatory changes which may or may not make the provisions of the Bill more or less useful.
I am sure the Minister will take this under advisement. In any event, I am sure he has taken the advice of his own administrators and advisory committee which recommended a

June 20, 1985
Western Grain Transportation Act
delay in the completion of the review period for at least two years. They recommended this delay because the changes and effects appeared to be greater and different from those contemplated by the former regime. I suspect the Conservatives plan even more changes, although the Minister has not dared to bring them in because they would open up other parts of the Act with which perhaps he does not want us to deal at this time. He does not want us to talk about Section 45, which brings me to the whole issue of variable rates. I presume the Minister received, yesterday or this morning, the written submission of the three prairie wheat pools. I do not know why he is reluctant to have us deal with Section 45. The former Minister, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy), built in enough protection against variable rates to last him until after the election. That time has run out, as has the protection.
Last year CN applied under the minimal protection of Section 45(2) to offer lower rates. When CTC demanded proof that it would benefit farmers, the railway withdrew its application. However, starting this December there will no burden of proof and the variable rates nightmare will be upon us again.
It is our position that if railroads want to set a lower rate to move grain under certain circumstances, for example on weekends or in slack time periods during the shipping season, that if they lower the rate for one grain producer, they must lower it for all grain producers. There should be no discrimination. The wheeling and dealing between CN and Northern Transportation Limited in an attempt to obtain a variable rate on a certain part of trackage in central Saskatchewan might be nice and might reduce the costs of grain producers along that line. However, what about grain producers along other lines? It is discriminatory and unfair. Railroads should not be allowed to do it. Certainly, they should not be allowed to apply for variable rates until the grain transportation committee is in place and has had time to do a lot of work, and until the review period has been completed.
The three pools made a recommendation in their submission indicating that Section 45(2) be amended as it did not apply prior to the completion of the comprehensive review in Part V, Section 62 of the Act, particularly Section 62(b).
I regret to advise the Hon. Member that his time has expired, unless the House chooses to let him continue by unanimous consent. Is there unanimous consent?
Agreed.
The House has given the Hon. Member unanimous consent.

Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleagues for their consideration. I just want to complete my remarks on the variable rates and on one other small matter before I resume my seat.
The three wheat pools went on to indicate that that Section did not apply prior to the 1986-87 crop year, except in respect
of a lower rate which would, in the opinion of the commission, encourage and reflect efficiencies gained from the loading or unloading of railway cars on weekend. Given that the legislation also calls for a comprehensive review in 1985-86, which included the entire Section relating to the rate scale, it is their belief that Section 45(2) was included with the understanding that Section 45(1) would not apply until the general review had been undertaken and completed. We cannot have a ridiculous situation where there is an ongoing review and the railroads open up the nightmare again with applications for variable rates.
I hope the Minister will consider bringing in the amendment at committee which the three prairie wheat pools requested. Perhaps he does not want us to deal with Section 62 relating to a full-scale review next year. That is much too soon to be of any real value in determining the effects of the legislation. We think that it should go back an additional crop year or two, so that the vagaries of prairie weather and the differences in productions and export sales over the previous two or three years could be taken into account and that there will be no adverse effect upon the review period itself.
Before the election the Minister, when he was trying to convince western farmers that they would be protected by the Conservatives, said that he wanted a three-year moratorium on rate increases. That was better than nothing, but where is it today? It is a freeze at the higher level of the 1984-85 crop year. In order to keep his commitment to western grain producers, I think he will accept our suggestion that the maximum rate should be that of 1985-86 and should apply for the two subsequent crop years.
In conclusion, I say to the Minister that we will have three or four amendments. I will endeavour to get copies of them to him today or tomorrow, as we have not quite finished preparing them. This will provide him with an opportunity to look at them before discussing them with us when the committee meets to consider this bill next Tuesday, I presume it is. I assure him that we think the improvements in the Bill outweigh its deficiencies. We are hoping that he will agree to some changes and additions to the legislation which we believe would make it even better in correcting some of the things that are wrong in the original Western Grain Transportation Act.

The House proceeded to the consideration of Bill C-26, an Act to amend the Old Age Security Act, as reported (without amendment) from the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.

Let me indicate to Hon. Members that I have had the opportunity to examine Motion No. 1 and Motion No. 2 on the Notice Paper in amendment at the report stage of Bill C-26, an Act to amend the Old Age Security Act. I have found them both procedurally in order and therefore intend to group them for debate. A vote on Motion No. 1 will apply to Motion No. 2.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of National Health and Welfare) moved:
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Motion No. 1
That Bill C-26, be amended in Clause 1 by striking out lines 10 to 14 at page 1 and substituting the following therefor:
"lived with that person for at least one year,"
Motion No. 2
That Bill C-26, be amended
(a)	by renumbering Clause 11 as subclause I 1(1)
(b)	by adding immediately after line 2 at page 9 the following:
"(2) For the period commencing on the day this Act is assented to and ending on August 31, 1985, the definition "spouse" in section 2 of the Old Age Security Act shall be deemed to read as follows:
" "spouse", in relation to a pensioner, includes a person of the opposite sex who has lived with the pensioner for at least one year and the pensioner and that person have publicly represented themselves as man and wife;"."

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in this very important debate on Bill C-26. We all know the admirable objective of this legislation which is to enable the elderly, that is, widows and widowers between the ages of 60 and 65, to receive the Old Age Security pension or the supplement, and we in the Liberal
Old Age Security Act
Party are very pleased with the Bill, but we do have a problem with certain discriminatory provisions.
Mr. Speaker, a Government that discriminates on the basis of marital status is not acting according to the spririt and the letter of the Canadian Constitution. Mr. Speaker, this very Parliament made a commitment not to indulge in any discrimination on the basis of language, sex, and so forth, and now one of the Government's first pieces of legislation is in fact telling single people who are members of a religious order, for instance, that they will not be eligible for pension benefits when they turn 60. Just because they decided to dedicate their lives to the education of our young people, and to the community, they will have to wait until they are 65. We are telling divorced individuals who have had problems during their working lives, problems in their marriages-Mr. Speaker, this is fairly common-that they are being penalized for not sticking with their husband or wife. That is what we are telling them. We are saying: no, no, no!
Imagine, Mr. Speaker, around the card table at the senior citizens' club, a women who is 61, whose husband died during World War II and her partner who got a divorce because while her husband was away from home, he found himself a young chick-
Such language!

The first woman is getting a pension and the second is not. That is the kind of situation you will hear about at the senior citizens' club in Saint-Hyacinthe. That is the kind of situation the Minister of State (Youth) (Mrs. Champagne) will have to explain to senior citizens in her riding. Why penalize people who were divorced or separated on perfectly legitimate grounds? Mr. Speaker, you will agree that this is intolerable. We cannot afford to discriminate in this way. I know, and I am very pleased to see the Minister of State (Youth), because although she is very busy with youth, she is also concerned about senior citizens because she has their respect. I know she cannot go along with these provisions, that she will go to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) and tell him: You do not realize what you are doing. Do you realize you are going to cause quarrels among old friends? They are going to be watching you. Mr. Speaker, these women unfortunately do not always have the resources to defend themselves. They are not always in a position to come and demonstrate or let the Government know the error of its ways.
Mr. Speaker, we all know that old age means a lot of loneliness. There are elderly women sitting in their living rooms right now who are wondering why they are being penalized because they were separated from their husbands and why they are being penalized because they got a divorce, for all kind of reasons. Is it up to the Government to make that kind of moral judgment? That is what I cannot tolerate in this Government. I cannot tolerate that people make judgments on

June 20, 1985
Old Age Security Act
the marital status of individuals. And that is what we are doing. If we did not intend to do this, why not say: We have the resources to do so much. That is, reduce the eligible age across the board to 64, 63 or 62. Do it in stages, but be fair. Be fair, because you will soon realize that people in our communities and in senior citizens' clubs across the country are going to be upset when they realize they are getting a raw deal because of their marital status. How dare you brand these people who have had problems in their lives? This is something I cannot tolerate. I think life has been hard enough on them already without the Government adding to their burden.
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart) engaged in a heroic struggle to try and make Government Members understand this. He circulated petitions across the country, and not even the thousands of signatures on these petitions were able to make this Government budge one bit, a Government that is obviously too insensitive to budge. Ever since they came to power, Mr. Speaker, they have been attacking the elderly in our society. We are not going to stand for that. We cannot tolerate a Government that has no respect for the people who built this country. We cannot tolerate that people who made sacrifices for years and years so they could give us the Canada we know today should be penalized either by de-indexation or because of their marital status.
Unfortunately, we are faced with a dilemma: we want to help widows and widowers, and we are sorry for those who are single, separated or divorced. Imagine the case of a single person who has helped his parents and his brothers and sisters all his life, and in fact given up his personal life to help them, and who today is being penalized for having made that sacrifice. Imagine the case of a person who got a divorce for whatever reason and who today wonders: What did I do wrong? Why will the Government not give me my pension and why is someone else who is widowed entitled to one? Imagine the problems in implementing Bill C26! Departmental officials are already telling us it is impossible to implement. Imagine the case of a person who was widowed recently or someone who has not heard from her husband for years. Is she separated? Is she widowed? Mr. Speaker, a distinguished lawyer like yourself will know that the application of a discriminatory piece of legislation creates all sorts of legal problems and I do not understand why the Government did not extend the application of this Bill to everyone.
Mr. Speaker, my colleague from Montreal-Sainte-Marie, to whom I want to pay homage because if there is one Member in this House who is concerned for senior citizens, he is the one, has organized a major operation called "Justice pour person-nes agees". I am convinced that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) will agree that his Bill is discriminatory. He even raised the issue himself by wondering what the courts could do if its application were to be questioned.
Mr. Speaker, we have had many opportunities to debate this matter in the House and I do not understand why not one single Member on the other side seems to share our concerns. I cannot believe that it is only in Liberal constituencies that there are single, separated or divorced people! For my part, I know that in the riding of Brome-Missisquoi, there are many single, separated and divorced people, and I do not understand why their Member of Parliament, who has a lot of influence with the Minister of National Health and Welfare because of her duties, did not come to their defence. I am still waiting for her speech in this House to defend people living alone, just as I am still waiting for her speech on the indexation of old age security pensions. I have read her statements with great disappointment, but this Bill was introduced to correct an unfair situation as we all know that people living alone face more hardship and are in a more difficult financial situation. However, in trying to correct one injustice, this Bill has created another one which is even more serious. Mr. Speaker, this is what we find difficult to accept, and I hope that, after having had the opportunity to listen to our many representations, our colleagues will reconsider and admit that you cannot discriminate against older people on the basis of their marital status.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak briefly to the amendment to the Old Age Security Act which I put forward for consideration today at report stage of Bill C-26. The amendment concerns the definition of common-law spouse in Bill C-26.
As the Bill is currently drafted, the definition of common-law spouse requires that there be a public representation as husband and wife with a cohabitation period of at least three years where there is a bar to marriage and if there is no bar to marriage, this period is reduced to one year. With this amendment to Bill C-26, the Old Age Security Act, the definition of common-law spouse will simply state that the minimum cohabitation period required is one year.
When I spoke on Bill C-26 at second reading stage, I raised this matter as I could not see any reason that a distinction between common-law spouses who had a bar to marriage and those who did not might be of significance. In fact, it merely serves to discriminate against a small portion of potential beneficiaries. I am sure this discrimination was completely inadvertent, but I am pleased to have this opportunity to correct it.
As well, this amendment brings the Old Age Security Act in line with another piece of legislation which is currently at committee stage, Bill C-47, an Act respecting divorce and corollary relief. I would like to mention a couple of points that have come up. It should be clearly understood that this allowance is subject to an incomes test. The other thing I would like to point out is that it will go a long way toward assisting spouses who are between the ages of 60 and 64 inclusive who have lost their partners and have been dis-
June 20, 1985

criminated against in the past. This amendment will ensure fairness in the application of the Act.
Because of the words of the previous speaker, I would like to mention one other thing. It is the intention that when this series of Acts is completed, it will be possible for two women to be drawing an allowance, one the legal wife and the other the common-law wife. After all, the reason they are drawing allowances is because they are both between the ages of 60 and 64. Although they are products of the shattered marriage, there is no difference in their need. Consequently, it would be possible for both of them to draw the allowance.
I would like to thank the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) for allowing me to speak to this amendment. I would suggest that it would be appropriate to hear from the Hon. Member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mrs. Bertrand) who will present Motion No. 2 standing in her name.

Mr. Speaker, I am both pleased and sad to rise to speak to Bill C-26. I am pleased, for we will speak before the present "minister of social injustice" and the former Minister of National Health and Welfare-
They are not listening!
-in the Conservative Government of Mr. Clark who is now the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Crombie). I wish he were still Minister of National Health and Welfare-
Hear, hear!

-because he was much more open. Mr. Speaker, I can understand why the "minister of social injustice" would rather not listen to my remarks, for he knows I am right.
Mr. Speaker, I support the amendment under consideration. But with respect to the principle of the Bill-
He is talking about you guys!

-it still is a measure which discriminates against people living alone and others who are single, separated or divorced. As a token of appreciation on the part of this Conservative Government, 80,000 people in Canada will soon find out that they are being penalized and ineligible for the spouse's allowance-and 80 per cent of them are women- simply because they are single, separated or divorced.
As we have seen in the current debate concerning the elderly and the deindexation of old age security pensions, it is more of the same from a Government which operates on the strength of opinion polls, makes hackneyed pronouncements, a faithful image of their leader the Prime Minister. When those people promised to make widows and widowers eligible for the
Old Age Security Act
spouse's allowance, it was simply because they had to say something during the election campaign to attract the elderly.
Since the Minister of State (Youth) (Mrs. Champagne) is in the House, I recall that she intervened during the election campaign after an article was published in the newspaper La Presse. She called a press conference right then and there to claim that the bad Liberals in her riding and the surrounding regions were saying that the Progressive Conservative Party would reduce old age security pensions. And I recall she had boasted that her Party would help widows and widowers as well as needy people living alone. I reacted immediately, called the journalist in question and explained to him that the Conservatives wanted to discriminate against people who are single, separated or divorced. The Minister of State then responded by saying: We will index pensions every three months. I said to the journalist: That is the way it is now. To that she replied: It is the Canada Pension Plan we will index every three months. I am not blaming her today, she did not know what this Government would do-deindex old age security pensions.
Do not put words in my mouth.

Mr. Speaker, if the Minister of State (Youth) wants it that way, I will get the newspaper articles, it is all there in black and white. If you want a debate on that issue, I would be pleased to argue with you.
On channel 10!
If I may, Mr. Speaker, I should like to get back to the Bill before the "minister of social injustice"-
He is not listening!

-and next to him his colleague the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. I like to give credit where credit is due, and if the present Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development who, in 1979, had agreed that the spouse's allowance should continue to be paid to the beneficiary when he or she became-

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. It may be due to the English translation, but I am wondering if it is appropriate for the Minister to be referred to continually as less than the Minister of National Health and Welfare. I wonder if that is appropriate conduct on behalf of the Hon. Member, as he is twisting the usage of a ministerial title.

speechtext:
