The Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie.

June 20, 1985
Old Age Security Act

Mr. Speaker, I do not know how people translate, but I translate the feeling of the people, what they think of the current performance of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp). They call him the Minister of Social Injustice-
This is not what he said!

All people in Canada.
[ Translation]
I will not repeat Mrs. Denis' comments, in which she voiced what she thought of the Prime Minister. You have read it in the papers.
So, Mr. Speaker, I would like to give credit to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Crombie) a Progressive Conservative Member who, when he was Minister of National Health and Welfare in 1979, decided and rightly so, with the support of the Liberal Party and the New Democratic Party at the time, to maintain the spouse's allowance after one of the spouses had deceased. At that time we, Liberals, said in committee: We are in agreement with that, Mr. Minister, but will your measure be retroactive because those who were not eligible before will be penalized? The Minister had given an open, gentlemanly answer: "Yes, that is reasonable. If you will allow me, I will go back to the Cabinet, because this involves extra expenditures, and I will return to you with an answer". The then Minister-he was not a Liberal but a Progressive Conservative Minister-was discharging his responsibility as a Minister of National Health and Welfare should, as the defender of senior citizens, of poor families-
Charlie Brown.

-of persons in need as Mrs. Begin did so well, my colleague is saying. It must be added to the credit of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development who was then Minister of National Health and Welfare, a determined man who won his point in Cabinet and everybody celebrated, not because it was a Liberal or a Progressive Conservative or a New Democratic victory, but because it was obtaining social justice for our seniors. Sadly, Mr. Speaker, I gave courteous notice to the current Minister of social injustice. Before the Christmas holidays, I started with that. Honestly, I believed it was a technical oversight, everybody being subject to human error. The Minister of National Health and Welfare was forewarned. I made representations. Some groups appeared before the Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs and they all expressed the same views. It was at the time when the Prime Minister, this government and even the Minister of social injustice were bragging that unlike the former government they were going to consult. All the groups came here, but the Minister did not budge. Not only was the minister unable to win his case in Cabinet to help women of 60 and 62 years of age, single, separated or divorced
persons, maybe he did not have the guts to attend the meetings, but he only tried to sell the stories of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and act as spokesman for high finance in Ontario. He did not fulfil his role which was to act fairly towards our senior citizens in need. Never mind the rich people. One of my constituents, a battered woman, now abandoned by her husband, made sacrifices to rear her children alone and pay for their education. She is living on welfare alone, which does not mean below the poverty line but rather below the extreme poverty line. The present Minister of National Health and Welfare answered that woman as follows: My dear lady, I understand your concern, but the government will continue to help you through social welfare. In other words, what it means is: "My dear lady, you are poor and you find it difficult to make ends meet, but you should find solace in the thought that you are always on our mind". The government absolutely refuses to act to remedy the situation.
There is a 63 year old lady, a Mrs. Denis who lives in the vicinity and who does not belong to any senior citizens group who came yesterday on Parliament Hill to give the Prime Minister a piece of her mind, just like that, simply because she was outraged. When she spoke, she expressed what each and every senior citizen in this country feels about the Prime Minister and his government. This is not something we should be proud about, for the Parliamentary system and people involved in politics really suffer when a Prime Minister is taken to task like that. And if we suffer, it is because of the actions of a number of individuals. We have now reached the report stage. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) again will have the opportunity to correct me if I am wrong when I say that his responsibility is not to stand up for big business, but that he is here to do what Mrs. Begin, his predecessor and former Minister of Social Affairs, used to do and what a Conservative colleague of his did more recently, namely, to stand up in Cabinet and ask for additionsl funds to help these people. The Minister of National Health and Welfare is well aware that when he grants the spouse's allowance, which is similar to the Old Age Security pension for those on Social Welfare, the government gives with one hand and saves 50 per cent with the other. The Minister is indeed well aware of that. It has nothing to do with party politics; it is simply a matter of social justice for all the people concerned.
I remember, on Remembrance Day, the three party leaders and their supporters in the House rising to pay tribute to those who had lost their lives on the battlefield. I wondered at the time who was going to take care of all these women who had to live away from their husbands who had gone to war and who had suffered because of the war, and whom the government rewards today with a firm "No". In each and every riding of this country, there is at least one person between 60 and 62 years of age who is single. She is generally the eldest in a family of some 10 children who has spent her live in a rural
June 20, 1985

community and quit school very early to help her parents raise her brothers and sisters. And now, having paid her dues to society, she has to try and find a job on the labour market, because she is told that she should have married and become a widow.
Mr. Speaker, I realize that my time is about to expire, but you can rest assured that I will continue to press my point when we deal with the next amendment.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Gabrielle Bertrand (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a second amendment to propose to Clause 11. This amendment would result in a change to the Old Age Security Act to reduce the period of cohabitation to one year in the case of common law unions, which change would come into effect immediately after Royal Assent. Without this amendment, the present definition requiring a minimum of three years of cohabitation where there is an obstacle to remarriage would remain in effect until September and deprive a number of people who have been living in such a situation for over a year and less than three from being eligible to make use of this provision.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words on Bill C-26 this afternoon as well. First, let me say that I am pleased that under the provisions of Bill C-26, approximately 85,000 widows and widowers in this country will now receive the spouse's allowance. Those 85,000 people, of course, are primarily women. I come from a riding in Saskatchewan which is very much a rural riding. It has a lot of small towns and villages and there are a lot of retired farmers. As I travel through those small towns in rural Saskatchewan I find that in home after home there is a woman living by herself. For some reason, women tend to outlive men, perhaps particularly in Saskatchewan. I find there is a tremendous amount of poverty among those women in my riding. They are living in dire straits with very little to live on. Life is very difficult for them. There have been many sad cases in my riding year after year where a spouse has passed away-almost certainly the man-and the wife is left with no money whatsoever. She has had to turn to social services to get some money in order to buy her daily food, to pay her heating bills or to buy clothing. So, Mr. Speaker, I welcome, indeed, the Bill which is before the House today in terms of the fact that it will provide a spouse's allowance for some 85,000 people.
At the same time, Mr. Speaker, I would like to reiterate the argument our Party has made many times before in this House with respect to pensions. I think primarily, of course, of the person who sat near me for many years in the House of Commons, Mr. Stanley Knowles, the former Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre. He made many, many speeches in this House with respect to pensions. He was the champion sans exception of the cause of pensioners in Canada. Before him, of
Old Age Security Act
course, there was J. S. Woodsworth, the former national Leader of the CCF who also made the cause of pensions a very important issue. If we go back to the beginning, we find that it was Mr. Woodsworth and a few Hon. Members of this House, along with the Liberal Government of Mackenzie King, who decided to bring in the first pension plan in Canada. It happened at that time to be a minority Parliament and Mr. Woodsworth and his colleagues in those days said, "We'll keep this Government in power for a little while in return for some good progressive legislation for Canadians", and the primary result of that legislation was the first old age pension plan in this country. The pension was very small. It did not take effect until, I believe, age 70, and there was a means test attached to it. But because of J. S. Woodsworth and a small group of Hon. Members of Parliament many years ago using their power in a minority Parliament as leverage, we received in this country our first old age pension plan.
The legacy was passed on when Mr. Woodsworth passed away and, in a by-election in 1942, Stanley Knowles was elected to this House. He took up the cause of championing the needs of senior citizens and pensioners in this country. He made speech after speech in this House over the years about the problems senior citizens face. He tried to get the pensions improved so that the people who built this country, who laid its foundation, could live in dignity. He made many speeches about the problems of widows and widowers and the fact that many of these people do not have money to live in dignity in these small towns and cities of our land. So it is his legacy, I suppose, that we bring into this debate today.
One thing I am sure he would have pointed out is that, in a way, this legislation is really discriminatory because it applies only to widows and widowers between the ages of 60 years and 65 years. If a person is between the ages of 60 and 65 and is divorced, he or she does not qualify for the spouse's allowance. If a person is between the ages of 60 and 65, is single, has never been married, even though he or she is poor and would qualify on the basis of the means test, he or she would not qualify because of not being a widow or widower.
I ask you, Mr. Speaker, in this 20th century, having proclaimed a few months ago Section 15 the equality section of the Charter of Rights, are we doing the right thing? We are discriminating on the basis of marital status, on the basis of whether it is a marriage in the traditional sense or a common law marriage. The amendments moved in the House today will, I guess, bring this legislation in line with the Divorce Act, which will become law in this country in a few months time. I just wonder whether it is right and proper that we should have that kind of discrimination built into the Bill which is before us today, although, as I said before, I support extending the spouse's allowance to those 85,000 Canadians who need it, many in my own riding and most of them women, I would assume. It relieves these women who have no other source of income of having to make that trip downtown to ask for social aid.
I think as far as it goes, Mr. Speaker, this legislation is a very good move. This legislation will cost, I believe, $190

June 20, 1985
Old Age Security Act
million in the next year, and in the first year it comes fully into effect it will cost $300 million. I think that is a very good thing in terms of those 85,000 people. But when it comes to the single people of this country-and according to statistics there are a lot of single poor, both men and women, living in big cities in small one-room apartments, living in small towns in little tiny houses-between the ages of 60 years and 65 years and unable to work,-those people will not qualify. Why is it that a married person should qualify over someone who is not? That really makes me hesitate. Why is it that someone divorced because of incompatibility or whatever, would not qualify while her next door neighbour, whose husband has passed away, would qualify even though she has exactly the same kind of background and economic ability to pay her own way? I think we should look at those very important questions.
What I would like to argue for, Mr. Speaker, is bringing down the pension age year by year to the age of 60 for everyone, and it should be universal just as medical care in this country is universal. The basic old age pension is now universal for people at the age of 65 years or over. I think we should bring down, one year at a time, as their country can afford it, the pension age to age 60 years for each and every citizen and not just for widows and widowers who happen to live in poverty.
This benefit also, of course, has attached to it a means test. One receives the spouse's benefit if one needs it because one has very little or no other source of income. Of course, we all want to help people in our society who are in need. We hear Hon. Members of the House and members of the media sometimes saying, "Why does Pierre Trudeau need a pension? Why does someone that wealthy need a pension?" Why does the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) need a pension? He is probably a pretty good farmer and will be a fairly wealthy guy when he becomes 60 years of age.
Why does Ed need a limousine?

I did not hear the interjection but I believe it was confirmation of the Minister of Transport's wealth. The arguments are made that we should take all this money and spend it on the poor in this country. But the problem with that, Mr. Speaker, is that we then have to establish a means test. We would have a ruthless division of classes in our country- one that has and one that has not-and that creates a lot of turmoil.
Are you arguing for or against a pension for me?

I am arguing for a pension for him regardless of his wealth, regardless of how much money he may or may not have, because they should be universal. That is my whole point. I support this Bill because it helps 85,000 widows and widowers, but I do so with a certain amount of hesitation. It discriminates against single and divorced people. The concept of universality is once again going out of the window. Regardless of one's background, we should all qualify for the pension. If you have children, you should qualify for the family allowance. If you are an older and poorer person, whether you are married or single, you should still qualify for the spouse's allowance. That is what I hesitate about regarding this Bill. So I urge the Minister to bring in legislation as soon as possible which does not discriminate against single or divorced people.
I want to conclude by quoting the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) when she spoke to the House on May 10, 1984, when she was in the Official Opposition. She said:
The fact that we have 600,000 elderly Canadians living in poverty in a country as rich and bountiful as Canada, in a society supposedly as compassionate and humane as ours, is a national disgrace.
We have a lot of senior citizens living in poverty. She said it was over 600,000. A recent Ontario report said that 42 per cent of pensioners in Ontario live in poverty.
There will be more with the new Government.

I conclude by asking the Government, why is it partially deindexing pensions for these people when it has those facts, when it knows about the suffering and misery? Why is it doing this when this will put more people into poverty, with those who are poor already becoming even poorer? I think the Government should listen to the sentiments of the Hon. Member for Kingston and The Islands and apply them while in government. If not, this will be a one-term Government, and that might indeed be the best thing for the people of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, while listening to the Hon. Member it came to my mind that the government Department which deals with social housing, the CMHC, just announced the closure of about 17 offices across the country and the downgrading of another 17. One of those was in the Minister's riding in Kingston.
I think most of the important points have been made by previous speakers and perhaps I could just add a couple of things which have not been mentioned. Whenever I hear someone talking about extending or increasing pensions to people over the age of 60,1 always think about those people in institutions subsidized by the federal and provincial Governments. Regardless of what pension increases the House of Commons votes quarterly, or of what extension is granted to new groups of people, it should be kept in mind that people in institutions such as senior citizens' homes or nursing homes in Newfoundland or anywhere else, see no increases. If you say that you are extending or increasing the pension as of January 1, they do not see an increase. They listen to the news and hear that they are going to qualify now for an additional pension or that their pension is being increased, but they do not see the increase. The point is that the money these people receive is determined by the provinces and is called a comfort allowance.
It is a strange system we have which makes how much money you receive from the federal Government depend on the
June 20, 1985

province you are in. It depends upon the decision of the provincial administration. I suppose you could go right through our social security system and you would see the same principle in effect.
I have listened to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) and other speakers talk about this measure being income tested. As one speaker outlined, possibly two people could qualify, one being the legal or common-law spouse of the other. In that situation I can see disputes arising and appeals being made to the Department of National Health and Welfare. Well, there is a principle that the Department has been following which is very confusing. I suppose, for the sake of federal-provincial relations, since the new Government took over, it is a good thing. I am referring specifically to pensions from that particular Department which are in dispute or under appeal. Regardless of whether it is the OAS, the GIS, or the allowance under this Bill, a disability pension or whatever, if the appeal, say, takes a year and the persons concerned received social assistance in the meantime, that is, welfare, they are not told that what they are to receive will have first gone to the provincial Department of Social Services concerned.
Since the new Government took over this is done in two days. Either the provincial Department hears about the person applying and goes directly to the Department of National Health and Welfare and tells them they owe us x number of dollars from that person's cheque retroactive to such and such a date, or else the social assistance officer goes to the individual who qualifies for the federal payment and says, "We want you to sign on the dotted line that you received x number of dollars from us and we are going to recover that from the Department of National Health and Welfare". As I say, it is good for federal-provincial relations but is not very good for the person who qualifies for the pension. You could have someone who is owed $8,000 in disability payments by the federal Government because his claim goes back four years, but he is then sent a message that his cheque has been sent to the provincial Government so that they can claim all the money he received from the Department of Social Assistance.
The Government has done something else with which I vehemently disagree. Since the Government came into power it has centralized in Ottawa the sending of cheques to people from this federal government Department. Since March 31, people in the Province of Newfoundland have not received their cheques on time. They have been a week or nine days late because of that change in administration. I suppose the post office is at fault, but certainly the Minister of National Health and Welfare can go to the Minister responsible for the post office to ensure that those cheques arrive on time.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare should realize, as should every Cabinet Minister, that everyone receiving a pension from this government Department is expecting it on a specified date. I have received letters from people saying that for the first time they had to go to the local merchant to
Old Age Security Act
borrow food while waiting for a cheque for which they never had to wait before. The Minister of National Health and Welfare should look into that matter. The shortcomings of this legislation have been pointed out and perhaps the Government will open its eyes and extend this benefit to everyone between the ages of 60 and 65.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to join in the debate on Bill C-26, an Act to amend the Old Age Security Act. It is a very important piece of legislation which goes some way toward correcting an imbalance in society but, in our view, it does not go far enough. The Government indicated that it was going to make this change on November 5, 1984, but it will not be implemented until September. It will take the Conservative Government almost 11 months to implement a measure which could have been implemented last fall.

We can't implement when you are
filibustering.

Mr. Speaker, it was not we who scheduled six, seven, eight, or nine opposition days in a row. We had a great time telling the Government all the things it was doing wrong, but the Government was not bringing forth legislation. We would have been quite happy then, as we would have been last November, to have had this legislation implemented. However, the Government, in its collective Conservative wisdom, decided that it had to move slowly.
The Act which extends the spouse's allowance to all low-income widows and widowers between the ages of 60 and 65 excludes a large section of the population in that age group. I speak of those individuals who never married or became divorced or separated from their spouses. We are putting them into a separate category. Even though their income may be the same as that of a widow or widower, under this Bill they are not entitled to support from the people of Canada.
The real issue is whether we should be treating all people who are over 60 equally regardless of their marital status. I think we should. I would encourage the Government to ensure that this Act is changed to give all Canadians who are 60 years of age and over and need additional income the support that they deserve. I do not think it is fair to tell single, divorced, and separated Canadians who do not have enough money that they must go on welfare. These people have worked for years and years in the service of the country by keeping the economy moving. We have a responsibility to treat them in an equitable manner.
This issue was raised in a discussion paper entitled Equality Issues in Federal Law under the auspices of the Minister of Justice and Attorney General (Mr. Crosbie). I will quote one section which deals deals with the spouse's allowance program. It says:
The spouse's allowance program raises another issue. Currently the allowance is paid to the spouse of a pensioner between the ages of 60 and 64 and to the surviving spouse if the spouse in receipt of Old Age Security dies before the survivor reaches the age of 65. There is currently a proposal to extend this benefit to all widows and widowers between the ages of 60 and 64. However, if

June 20, 1985
Old Age Security Act
an individual is single, separated or divorced and aged 60-64, no allowance is paid, even if the individual's needs meet the test for benefit to spouses. A decision has been made to allocate funds to married couples as opposed to single individuals in the age bracket 60-64. One of the rationales for this is that unmarried persons can get assistance from provincial welfare programs, although they receive smaller benefits. Given that there are only limited resources to provide for needy people, this group was selected. The question is whether marital status is an appropriate reason for choosing between equally needy people, particularly when the criteria for receipt of an allowance is need.
There can be no difference, Mr. Speaker, need is need is need. If you need money to survive, it does not matter whether you have never been married or are now a widow or widower. Justice suggests that we should treat them equally.
In the last Parliament, a committee of the House examined pensions. There was a minority report filed by the former Member for Nanaimo-Alberni, Mr. Ted Miller. In it is a section entitled "People Under 65". It reads:
During the course of its hearings, the Task Force received submissions discussing the plight of people, largely between the ages of 55 and 64, who are ineligible for benefits under any public pension program. Though we had neither the mandate nor the time to examine the particular needs of this group, there was concern among witnesses and Task Force members that many people under 65 face severe hardships with little support from public sources.
These problems frequently include ineligibility for any sort of public pension benefits and long or frequent periods of unemployment. The community from where the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) comes and the community of Atikokan in my riding have endured the shut-down of basic industries. There are people who worked in those industries for 30 or 40 years who are still in their mid-fifties or early sixties and cannot get jobs. Even if the jobs were available, due to the severe conditions under which they worked in the mines, their bodies are not as willing or able as they used to be. If we were to provide some support for those who are 60 years of age and over, we would at least raise their standard of living.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I encourage the Government to accept our proposal and provide full justice for all who are 60 years of age and over in order that they too can get the income support which they need to survive in our society today.

Mr. Speaker, I am also very happy to take part in this debate on Bill C-26, which is in itself an excellent initiative for the people who will benefit from its provisions, namely the widows.
Nevertheless, I find this Bill clearly discriminatory and odious in the way it treats certain people.
During the last few weeks, many of my colleagues had the honour and the privilege of tabling a number of petitions which in their preamble deplored the discrimination and the class distinction the Government was making with respect to people who were separated, divorced or single. I think this aptly describes a situation that I find totally unacceptable and highly reprehensible.
Mr. Speaker, I shall, if I may, go back briefly in time, and recall that Canada's divorce legislation was originated by an Act of Parliament passed in 1968. At the time, and this is, after all, not so long ago, couples who had experienced a certain number of problems were being given a chance to legalize their situation. We must not forget that if a person who had the misfortune to have made an unhappy marriage for which there was absolutely no remedy, then decided to take advantage of this legislation, that person was almost automatically singled out and ostracized by the community. These are the people who will be hurt by Bill C-26. Because of the law and the attitudes of our society at the time, in 1968 and 1970, divorced persons were seen as people who were different, and families felt a sense of shame when a member of the family got a divorce. These are the people who today, in many cases, are over 60 years old. These are the very people who are being told today that because of the Budget, they are going to be deprived of what their friends will be entitled to because they are widows or widowers. So I think it is despicable to deprive these people of what in the circumstances would seem to be essential and fundamental.
We must also recall that in the late 60s and early 70s, in almost every divorce where there were children, custody was usually given to the mother. At the time, our social legislation was not as advanced as it is today, and here again, these women have been victimized, in addition to being branded as second-class citizens and having to suffer the ostracism of their neighbours and the effects this had on their relations in their community. They were responsible for the education of their children, they had very limited financial resources. These are the people who in many cases went through absolute hell, and today, now they are 60, they are being told that the provisions of Bill C-26 do not apply to them but if the economy improves, we might review the situation and consider the problem.
The fact that they are being excluded on such ridiculous grounds is, I think, an incredible insult to all these people who are divorced, separated or single. It is an unconscionable affront to these people who have the same rights and privileges as anyone else. It has often been said in this House, and rightly so, that the Canadian Constitution was so good for Canada because it prevented class distinction and put all Canadians on an equal footing.
In my opinion, in view of the way this Bill is designed, it is an extremely regressive measure. We are regressing 15 or 20 years in the past because of a measure which creates a social class of needy victims who have already been victimized in the past and on whom has now been placed an intolerable burden.
Everyone recognizes that 80,000 people will be penalized by the Bill and will be deprived of this assistance which, in many cases, their spouse will be able to obtain. Everyone also recognizes that the very great majority of these 85,000 people are women, women who have been fighting and organizing for
June 20, 1985

years to gain an equality, a justice and an equity which are still not apparent in this Bill.
I therefore believe that, as parliamentarians, we have a duty to ask this Government to put this whole issue back on the table and to consider granting these 80,000 people the most basic justice if we do not want them to become innocent victims.
Mr. Speaker, I hope that we shall witness a reversal on this issue within the next few days and that this will be followed by amendments which will ensure that these people will be treated more fairly.
This afternoon, an amendment was introduced to make common law spouses eligible for these benefits. If I may, I would like to enumerate all the problems which could be the result of trying to identify these people through such a mechanism.
Will the Government be able to intrude in the private life of people to determine whether they are entitled to the benefits or not?
My colleague is telling me with good reason that 80,000 people are being branded in Canada at a time where we are trying to see justice done and to make sure that all Canadians will be treated fairly according to the principles of social justice, and in closing I would like to ask all my colleagues to reconsider this issue and to try to understand what will be the life of these men and women who will be deprived of the benefits of Bill C-26 if it is not amended.
On a point of order, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to say a few words about this Bill which we support and, as you know, we do not intend to delay the proceedings at the report stage. I would simply remind the House that we are considering Motion No. 1 in the name of the Government to amend:
Old Age Security Act
Clause 1 by striking out lines 10 to 14 at page 1 and substituting the following therefor: "lived with that person for at least one year."
The effect of this amendment or this motion is of course to implement a recommendation of the committee and the Minister to reduce from three years-the previous requirement-to one year the time for becoming eligible under this measure. That is how it is going to be once the Bill is passed, it is defined as living together for one year.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few comments on Bill C-26 as well as on the significance of this amendment. As you may recall, Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this Bill is to extend the spouse's allowance program to needy people living alone and aged 60 to 64. Most people affected by this measure are women. It is therefore an important Bill which responds to a social and economic need in our society. However, Mr. Speaker, only widows and widowers are eligible under this Bill, so it excludes people who are single, separated or divorced. Again I say that 80,000 people between the ages of 60 and 64 would be eligible if the Government had been more generous towards them and had seen fit to establish a more extensive and comprehensive program. This measure therefore discriminates against certain people, most of them, I repeat, Canadian women aged 60 to 64 who fail to meet the spouse's allowance eligibility requirements.
Mr. Speaker, in my riding, and I find this example particularly striking because it was part of my life, there are many female members of religious orders who have taken a vow of chastity and live in a state of celibacy. These women are not eligible for the benefits provided under this Bill, because they do not meet the requirements: they are neither widows nor widowers-there are also male members of religious orders- and I think this discriminates against these people, should they, for whatever reason, wish to leave their religious order and live a secular life.
Mr. Speaker, the Progressive Conservative Government, which is so proud of its consultation policy, did not bother to consult people between the ages of 60 and 64 before tabling this measure, that I am sure of, because if they had, in the riding of Ottawa-Vanier at least they would have met a lot of women, single women who have worked hard in an environment that is not always easy, in a city like Ottawa that is largely dependent on Parliament,on the Government, a public service city. We all know that until recently, the majority of public servants-and it may still be the case today-have been women, many of of whom are between the ages of 60 and 64, and were left with an income or pension that puts them on the poverty line. If we had only bothered to think about these people, if we had considered all these women who in many cases have worked hard for very low salaries, and who are now retired and have no security, Mr. Speaker, and who today, we might as well admit it, are in many cases forced to depend on provincial or federal grants for housing, for medical drugs, for

June 20, 1985
Old Age Security Act
transportation, and for a host of other services which they would much rather pay for themselves.
Mr. Speaker, 1 just want to set the record straight on this piece of Government legislation which we are endorsing because it does extend an existing program to a substantial number of Canadians. However, once again, we earnestly request this Government to expand this measure to another
80,000	men and women who should be eligible but are not covered by this measure.

Unfortunately, while supporting the Bill-we will not delay it and I think I am the last one to speak on this side, although perhaps there is some other Member who might want to speak-I want to repeat the point again that I am disappointed and so are my colleagues in the Liberal Party that the measure is not extended to deserving Canadians, those who chose not to marry and those who are separated and divorced. They are the ones being excluded from this extended coverage. I regret that.
In my day-to-day meetings with constituents, men and women have said to me, "We feel disenfranchised". I say this with a lot of heart because they feel they are being left out of a very important program. We have tabled petitions. I have personally tabled several petitions asking the Government to reconsider this measure and to modify it so that these people who have chosen not to marry, who are divorced or separated can be included.
The Conservative Government, Mr. Speaker, has missed a golden opportunity for meaningful reform. It has wallowed in indecision. God knows that the Conservatives are undecided even on Old Age Security. Nobody knows where the Conservatives stand. One day you hear the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) say something and the next day you hear the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) say something else. Canadians, especially seniors, would like to have the assurance that this Government thinks about them, cares for them and will give them the security they deserve without adding anxiety, which is such a difficult and common feeling among our elderly. Anxiety is something seniors do not need. Anxiety has been created by the Conservative Government over these pensions. Anxiety has been created by indecision on the part of the Government as to where the Government is going and what it is going to do for the senior citizens.
If the Hon. Member on the other side has something to say, he should stand up and make a speech for 10 minutes. I will sit down and invite him to do so right now.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure again to participate in this debate. I think there are certain close parallels that reflect and mirror this piece of legislation and the pension issue in the recent Budget. It seems that to this Government numbers mean nothing. It seems that to this Government individuals mean nothing. We talk about thousands upon thousands of individuals who are between the ages of 60 and 64 some perhaps are not married, and some perhaps are separated or divorced. Do they mean less to the Government than those who have a different type of marital
status? We as a society cannot afford to discriminate among individuals on that sort of basis.
If we are prepared to move and move in a progressive direction as the Bill has done, we should be prepared to move progressively all the way for all individuals, recognizing that the problem facing a 64-year old married person is the same as the problem faced by the 64-year old woman in Sault Ste. Marie who may not be married or who is divorced. We must begin to realize that if we are prepared to recognize those problems and if we are prepared to say we have to help those between the ages of 60 and 64 because they cannot help themselves, then we cannot allow or afford to discriminate. We cannot allow marital status to dictate whether or not they receive something. The only basis for the decision should be need. If a divorced or separated person has that need, that financial compensation should be there as it is for married people.
We are losing sight of the lot of the individual. We are looking at it in terms of thousands. Perhaps when we look at it in that light, it simply becomes a statistic, and we throw statistics around loosely and easily. We should narrow it down to the lot of the individual, to the specific needs of individuals who feel and know that they are being discriminated against.
We have received letters from such individuals suggesting that they need the money as much as other people do. They ask why they are being kept out of it when other people are not. They are the same types of letters as the ones we are receiving on the pension issue, saying that we have to get our financial house in order, that Canada is a great country, that it is full of opportunity, but asking why the decision was made to bring down the deficit on their backs. Pensioners were told that their pensions were a sacred trust. A commitment was given that their pensions would not be touched or altered. We are involved in the same debate at this point, because we are talking about a commitment to people which should be honoured.
When we talk about commitment, we should also talk about consistency, honesty and integrity. If the Government is prepared to make that social contract with the elderly, if it is prepared to say to these people that it will not touch their pensions, then it ought to follow through on those commitments. Anything short of that is simply not good enough. That debate is very much relevant to and alive in Bill C-26. If we are prepared to tell Canadian society that we, as a Government and as a Parliament, are prepared to step in and offer assistance, we ought to cover the entire clientele. If we are not prepared to do that, perhaps I would rather not do what we are doing. I would rather not do it in a piecemeal fashion and at the same time boast and say how great we are because we are moving in such a direction. It ought to be done with some sense of compassion for all individuals who feel the need for that financial assistance.
Indeed, the Bill points in the right direction. I do not think anyone in the House of Commons would rise and suggest that
June 20, 1985

this is somehow completely unwarranted. It is moving in the right direction, but why not enlarge it and encompass the entire Canadian community? Why not enlarge it to make it more progressive? Why can the Government not admit that while it is moving in the right direction, that direction is not wide enough? Why can it not admit that while it is trying to satisfy the needs and aspirations of that community, it is not fulfilling all that is desired? Why can the Government not rise in its place and say that it will be extended to those individuals against whom the Bill discriminates? That is leadership, that is conviction. It would mean rising and admitting some shortcomings. It is the same argument that we have debated for the last two and a half weeks on the whole question of pension deindexation.
It is leadership to admit to the country that a mistake was made in the budget paper, that it was a regressive mistake and that the Government reneged on a promise. That is leadership. Leadership is not showing Canadians that it is prepared to be tough, not to back down, or that it is prepared to be arrogant, despite the pleas, calls, letters, protests and questions which have been asked during Question Period.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Would the Hon. Member please speak to the motions before the House?

Mr. Speaker, I thought I was. I was trying to indicate that on this particular motion the Government has an opportunity, which it could take, to make the Bill more compassionate and fair. That was the message I was trying to bring to the attention of the House, in an attempt to bridge the current debate which is gaining in public momentum on Bill C-26.
The Government should say that it is moving in the right direction but that that direction should be expanded to include individuals such as the ones who have written to us and perhaps to Hon. Members opposite. These individuals are asking the Government not to discriminate on the basis of whether they are divorced, separated or married. They say that the decision should be based upon need, fairness and age. If it is good for one 62-year old person of a certain marital status, it should be good for others.
I believe those are the issues on which Hon. Members in my Party and in the NDP have been rising. We are speaking to the fairness and legitimacy of this particular proposal. We cannot afford to allow a Bill to pass which discriminates against certain individuals. It is our task and responsibility to rise in our places, not merely to give the Bill our blessing, but to play the role for which we were elected. We do not mean to be obstructionist, but it is our role in the House to improve upon and comment upon legislation, and to point out a certain direction which we think the Government should take. Indeed, it would be leadership if the Government were prepared to expand the Bill to make it more progressive. If the Government did so, I am sure there would be no opposition; Hon. Members would not rise to talk on another subject related to the Bill. Reciprocal leadership would be displayed on the part of this Party. We would say that the Government did the
Old Age Security Act
correct thing and, therefore, we would give it speedy passage. That is leadership, not only on the government side but also on the opposition side.
I believe that the role of the Opposition is not to obstruct. It is to ensure that the legislation is what Canadians want, not what the Government wants, not what the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) or his Government may think Canadians want. When we talk about this particular issue, Canadian want fairness for all people who are 60 to 64 years of age, regardless of their marital status. When we talk about fairness, we are talking about pensioners who say; "Leave our pensions intact and give us full indexation".
The message for the Government on this Bill and on the pensions issue is: Let us provide some leadership and give Canadians the legislation they demand and rightfully deserve.
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. In that there is one minute remaining, could I ask a question of the Hon. Member who just sat down?
No.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I was about to ask for unanimous consent of the House, but I do not think the Hon. Member would get it.

Mr. Speaker, I want to speak on this Bill, particularly as it relates to the riding of Spadina. It extends, for low-income widows and widowers, the spousal allowance to about 85,000 people in Canada. Of course we support that. One has to; I am sure it will be unanimously supported.
This leads me to asking the following question: Why take a course which benefits a very limited number of needy people? There are many equally needy single and divorced people. In fact, for whatever reasons, there are a great many divorced people in Canada, many of whom are or will soon be of pensionable age. There is also a growing number of single people in the country. This benefit is being extended to a relatively small group and, in a sense, to a shrinking group, according to present population trends. This is very evident in the riding of Spadina. As between the 1971 census and the 1981 census in Spadina, there was a sharp increase in the number of single people. Most of these people will not ever be in line for the benefit of this legislation. Many of those have low incomes; many of those are going to be hurt by the Government's deindexation of the Old Age Security pensions next year and in the years ahead. Why does the Government try to kid the public by taking away with a shovel and putting back with a teaspoon? It takes away from all the pensioners in Canada, starting next January and increasing cumulatively every year, $100 a year, then $200 a year, then $300 a year and so on. It takes that away from them and then it undertakes to give back to a few.
If the country were as poor as the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) tells us it is, perhaps it would be justified to say

June 20, 1985
Old Age Security Act
that it can only give to a few, although it is not clear why it should be given to a widower and not to a divorced person. Why is a widower or a widow more needy than a divorced person, or a single person? That is not clear. Of course, in fact the country is not anywhere nearly as poor as the Prime Minister has said. This country makes huge tax gifts to people who need such gifts very little or not at all. It makes them on the worn out, discredited claim that those people will use the money to create jobs. That is a theory that the former Liberal Government worked to death during the last dozen years, and this present Tory Government is doing the same thing, to take from the senior citizens in order to give to the friends of the Government and to try to cover what it is doing by giving back a little bit to a tiny number of senior citizens.
The people in Spadina are not fooled. They are not amused. They have been out petitioning with a petition that states the facts clearly as to what will happen in 1986 and 1987. Generally-

speechtext: Order. Could I please ask the Hon. Member to be very, very specific at the report stage of the Bill at which we are and speak precisely on either Motion No. 1 or Motion No. 2?

Mr. Speaker, the reason why I am taking part in this debate is quite simple: it is somewhat the continuation of the debate held the other evening, and I am under the impression that the government still does not understand what it means to look after our less fortunate citizens.
You referred a while ago to relevancy and I will readily stick as much as possible to the proposal so that my colleagues will not have to call me to order.
I still have actual cases in mind. I have always thought that in politics one has to state one's case clearly, because people will only grasp the issues if one understands perfectly the purposes we are trying to achieve. Therefore, I will refer to some examples I gave the other evening about the homes located in my constituency, which you know quite well, Mr. Speaker, as I know yours also. There are homes for senior citizens in both our ridings.
The bill now under consideration is exclusively meant for people who have a status in the community, either widows or widowers, and my colleague from Montreal-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart), my colleague from Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier), my NDP colleague as well as my colleague from York have explained the matter very clearly. People of the same age are excluded because they have a different status, and now we are told that if they have been living together for one year, they may qualify. But I know of specific cases involving people that I met, and I know that this is also a problem for my colleagues in this House.
The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mrs. Bertrand) knows of many such cases in her constituency. My friend and colleague from Terrebonne (Mr. Toupin)-I could name them all-we have the same kind of people and the same kind of problems. The actual problem in a home that I will call, for example, Berri-Lajeunesse, in Montreal, is that people there have little money and managed, as I said recently, to find a place to live, let us say apartment 404, and because they have a different status, they get a pension, unlike their neighbour who is divorced or separated or still, which is most unfair, who is single. I would like to draw the attention of my colleagues especially to the case of the single woman. We all know, we especially from Quebec, and I would like to draw the attention of my English-speaking colleagues-

-especially from Quebec, who have known in the past, not at this time and not in the future unfortunately, but in the past. There was always one person in these families who sacrified most of the time for all kinds of reasons but whom happened to be the one who did not get married, because Therese, Pauline, Celine and Marc looked after papa and mama, after grandpapa and grandmama. There was always one in our families. The example could be multiplied; in every district you will find that. These people have consecrated-

-devoted their lives taking care of their old parents while others have married and those who have married, who have raised children, who have even become widows or widowers, will qualify. But their sisters or brothers who remained single cannot qualify. I hope I have very well understood the thrust of this legislation.
Mr. Speaker, at first glance, we find this shocking, deplorable. I want to warn my friends opposite: We will support the legislation... Why? Because we want to give more money to people who have long been ignored, but still we cannot refuse to consider a group which will benefit immediately. This is why I assure you ... I did not consult anyone but I think the agreement is... we will vote for this legislation as soon as possible, probably today or tomorrow or within the next few
June 20, 1985

days. But still I would like this House to consider the situation of those who have been ignored, and as I said, the ones that are ignored so very often as we all know, and it has been said time and again, are mainly women, because they live longer-the average life expectancy being there to prove it-and most of all the lonely, single women. They are again being ignored in this legislation.
1 am aware that we are going to support this legislation. However, I would appreciate it so much if the Government, my colleagues, the most distinguished Member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mrs. Bertrand) when I say these things, I believe in them, and I know she can exercise her charming, composed and benevolent influence because this often is more productive with the Hon. Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp), the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney)-could be convinced that something will have to be done in the future for those who have been ignored by this legislation on which we are getting ready to vote today or tomorrow or in the days ahead as I said.
In my view, in the name of fairness, we must make good, I would not say that injustice but to say the least, that oversight.
There are so many things that could be said on that, Mr. Speaker, and 1 am somewhat amazed that there has been no reference to past experience.
When I first came here, several years ago, I remember very well, at that time, the universal pensionable age was 70 and all the political parties said ... and certainly, my honourable friend, the ever-charming and distinguished Member for Brome-Missisquoi and Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister will remember as well as I do that in our election platforms, we wanted to promise old age security pension at age 65. What did we do then? Under the leadership of an extraordinary Prime Minister, because I served under that man, the Right Honourble Lester B. Pearson-I have always been known to be a "Pearsonian", since very often one identifies oneself with the name of the Prime Minister under whom one was first elected. Then your new Members could be called "Mulroneyans", including you, Mr. Speaker-
Laurier!
-the "Trudeauists" ... My colleague says that perhaps it was under Laurier. I must recognize that he was and will remain in Canadian history one of our great Prime Ministers.
What about Laurier?

He understood very well. Laurier understood very well what Canada was all about. He better than anyone in this country understood absolutely how this country
Old Age Security Act
came about. If my colleague would like me to speak about Sir Wilfrid Laurier, I will do so some other time.
I remember that Lester B. Pearson made a proposal that was accepted. At that time, we thought we did not have enough money to give pensions to people who were between the ages of 65 and 70. Some Hon. Members here will remember that, and if I am wrong about it, and I do not think I am known to be too arrogant, I will not mind being corrected. I remember that the new plan of Mr. Pearson was that since we could not provide the money for everyone at that time, we would provide pensions that first year for all those who were 69 years of age. The next year-

speechtext: That's what we are doing now.

Yes, but to everyone. I want my hon. friend to understand that we provided pensions for everyone, not just the bachelors. The following year, we provided pensions for those who were 68, then 67, and then 66, and then we achieved the provision of pensions for everyone between the ages of 65 and 70. There was no discrimination. Now we are being asked to forget 80,000 people for the benefit of others who-

-are widows or widowers.
I think that the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare realizes now that there is something unfair about this legislation for our brothers and sisters who, althougth 60 to 65 years of age, are not eligible.
I am glad to repeat in front of my whip-

However, we can imagine the discrimination against some older people living in homes for the aged because it is even worse for senior citizens who live together than for those who live alone by themselves. In the same building, on the same floor, there are some senior citizens who get the pension and others who do not, simply because they are divorced or separated from a spouse who did not deserve them, or simply because they are single. These are the people who will be discriminated against as of September 1. Therefore, I ask, urge and beg the government to think these things over and to arrive at a solution with a view to avoiding a repetition of this unfortunate situation.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to take part in the debate on the amendment to Bill C-26. Our Party fully supports Bill C-26, but what we want as Liberal Members of the House is to make sure that the Bill does not leave any stone unturned and that as many Canadians as possible are protected under the provisions of this measure. I take this opportunity to congratulate my colleague the Hon. Member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Pru-

June 20, 1985
Old Age Security Act
d'homme) on the excellent speech he made in the House of Commons earlier today, and to commend the Hon. Member for Monteal-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart) for his work in this case. Mr. Speaker, objective and impartial as you are, you have certainly appreciated, and rightly so, the outstanding work done in this case by the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie and of course the Hon. Member for Saint-Denis. [English]
What we are talking about here today is something that will ensure that more people are protected by Bill C-26. In its present form, Bill C-26 will enhance the standard of living for certain Canadians, but it will create an injustice whereby some
80,000	Canadians will be discriminated against. There is no doubt that the Hon. Member for Longueuil (Mr. Leblanc) would agree with me that this is unfair. He would no doubt want to speak on behalf of his constituents, if he were permitted to do so, to state in the House that Bill C-26 would be much better if it applied to every Canadian in need between the ages of 60 and 64.
If a person between the ages of 60 and 64 is divorced or separated and has the same financial need as a person who is widowed, why should we want to discriminate against that person? I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that you, just like I, would not want to discriminate against single, divorced or separated Canadians. We would want all Canadians with little or no means to be provided with the financial assistance that they so richly deserve at an age when they have contributed so much to our society.
I have discussed the following issue in this House in the past, but I would like to repeat myself just in case some Hon. Members were not giving their undivided attention to me at that time. I know that I cannot say that I am doing this in case some Hon. Members were not present because all Members are always present in the House, as you have decreed in the past, Mr. Speaker. Just in case some Hon. Members were not paying attention when I raised this issue before, let me raise again the following proposition: it is a fact that single and divorced Canadians will be discriminated against because this Bill will not assist them.
Let me describe certain instances in which single Canadians will be discriminated against. If a Canadian citizen is divorced and is no longer receiving alimony or other benefits from a former spouse, potentially that person is in the same financial difficulty as a person who is widowed. Both of them have lost the person who assisted them financially.
In conclusion, I urge the Government to consider the Liberal amendment.

subsubtopic: CALL FOR RESTORATION OF FULL INDEXATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since gray power has come to the fore in Canada, elderly Canadians have been actively protesting the Tory Budget's intention to cut indexation next January and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has been looking to find a way to sneak out of that ill-founded policy. There are ways to do it. He can simply announce today, as he should, that the policy of deindexing has been dropped. He won't though, since such directness is not part of his style.
Already there are predictions that somehow, in the next few weeks or months, the Canadian economy will undergo some magical rejuvenation which will make deindexing unnecessary. Then the Tories will try to paint themselves as true-blue heroes. Nobody will be fooled, because Canadians will not allow themselves to be fooled again by the Tory gang.
Canadians are recalling the old saying: "Fool me once, shame on you; fool me twice, shame on me". No, Canadians will not allow themselves to be fooled again by the Tory gang and by the Prime Minister's lack of credibility.
When the announcement comes changing the deindexing provisions of the Budget, and it will, the Prime Minister or the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) will announce the change sitting down.
Now is the time for them to announce that deindexation will be discontinued.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw the attention of the House to a significant event which will occur in Windsor, beginning tomorrow. The most significant national holidays in Canada and the United States are July 1 and July 4 respectively. It was to commemorate these nearly coincident national days that the Windsor-Detroit International Freedom Festival was inaugurated by Queen Elizabeth II and Prince Philip in 1959. Since then it has grown to become the largest international festival in the world and is attended by millions from both sides of an undefended border which was once the destination of both my slave and abolitionist forefathers.
Occasionally there are fireworks in this House over relations between Canada and the United States because we, just as much as the Americans, take pride in our independence and freedom. In Windsor and Detroit next week we will have the largest annual display of fireworks in either country, when we, as two equal peoples, celebrate our friendship, freedom, and'
June 20, 1985

honour-heroes in the cause of human rights. We hope you all will come on down to the Banana Belt and have a good time.

subtopic: UNITED STATES STRATEGIC DEFENCE INITIATIVE-JOINT COMMITTEE DELIBERATIONS
UNITED STATES STRATEGIC DEFENCE INITIATIVE-JOINT COMMITTEE DELIBERATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for a number of weeks now, I, and I am sure all Members of Parliament, have been receiving letters and other communications from constituents in connection with the invitation to Canada from the United States to participate in the Strategic Defence Initiative research program.
While the letters started some time ago, the volume has increased dramatically since the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) indicated the Government's desire to consult with the Canadian people on the subject of SDI research.
Many Canadians are happy to write to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), or their Member of Parliament, but many more, including the East York Peace Committee, with which I recently met, are anxious for an opportunity to express their views before an all-party committee of Parliament. Party task forces have their place, but they are no real substitute for a parliamentary committee.
1 was delighted last week when all Parties set aside their differences and agreed to establish a Special Joint Committee of the Senate and the House of Commons to investigate the subject of Canada's participation in SDI research, and to report by August 23. That will provide a vehicle which will enable all Canadians to have an input into a decision which will be of enormous significance to us all.

Mr. Speaker, is the Parliamentary Press Gallery exercising responsible journalism? The very worthy Report on House of Commons Reform which was tabled this week is typified by The Globe and Mail as "a challenge to the Prime Minister". Columnist Don McGillvary says it won't work because the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) would have to "surrender power". These writers are either overly cynical, dim-witted, or perhaps both.
As a journalist who entered politics, I well remember the tendency of some journalists to become a self-ordained political opposition. Unfortunately, in recent years, the Parliamentary Press Gallery has not distinguished itself, both in quality and in intellect. Most Ottawa Press Gallery members pale in comparison with legislative and parliamentary reporters in other world capitals.
Our Press Gallery is preoccupied with controversy, division, and sensationalism. Because of this, the Press Gallery discourages the very kind of debate that it desires. Objectionable behaviour, unparliamentary language, rat packs, and disorder are the stuff of headlines in the national news.
Sensible, thoughtful, and intelligent debate in the House of Commons and in committee is seldom, if ever, reported. Most of this reasoned debate takes place before or after Question Period, when the media benches are entirely empty and the reporters have gone home.
Fairness, accurate portrayal, and balance are what jounal-ism is all about. It is time our Press Gallery woke up.

Mr. Speaker, I am shocked and disappointed that the federal Conservatives have broken yet another election promise regarding affirmative action to hire the handicapped. Groups representing hundreds of thousands of women, minorities, and handicapped, are profooundly upset and say that the Mulroney Government's proposed equity scheme has fundamental flaws and will fail.
The federal legislation should have responded to the Abella Royal Commission Report: Equality in Employment, but instead it will not contain any mandatory program for affirmative action, any mechanism for enforcing companies' compliance with the legislation, or even any mechanism to monitor the so-called law.
In this lip service approach, all a company will have to do is declare that it is an Equal Opportunity Employer, even though the Government knows that such voluntary action is branded as useless by all who are experienced in the field. Without proper monitoring, groups will have no basis for complaints.
To add insult to injury, only companies dealing in contracts of more than $200,000 will be eligible, instead of the $20,000 limit which was proposed in the Obstacles Report that was commissioned by the Liberal Government. An enormous number of companies which do business with the Government will be left out completely from complying. The new law will be absolutely toothless.
Kathleen Ruff, of the Canadian Association for the Mentally Retarded, stated on June 12, 1985:
-this is not employment equity, this is misleading advertising, this is a dishonest statement on the part of the Government. It is a broken promise.
Jim Derksen, National Chairman of the Coalition of Provincial Organizations of the Handicapped, said June 19-

June 20, 1985

Mr. Speaker, Herman "Jackrabbit" Johanssen has reached the venerable age of 110 years and is celebrating that fact at a large party which will be held this afternoon.
He is convinced that his long life is the result of the skiing and canoeing he enjoyed after he came to Canada in 1902.
"Jackrabbit" Johanssen certainly provides splendid evidence of the beneficial effects of such athletic activity.
Although canoeing was developed by the native peoples during their long centuries on this continent, Canadians should be grateful to Mr. Johanssen and other Scandinavian immigrants for their introduction of skiing to our country.
Cross-country skiing has become a vital part of winter life in many Canadian communities. Mr. Johanssen's contributions to that have been recognized at the Canadian Ski Museum in Ottawa.
Entire families enjoy cross-country skiing in my city of Thunder Bay, and sport organizers there have been working hard to bring the World Nordic Games to our community. Participation in these amateur sports does much to improve the fitness of Canadians and to extend the vital life of senior citizens.
The desire of seniors to lead a full life depends on the incomes which are provided by adequate pensions. Mr. Johanssen joins with other seniors, and most Canadians, in demanding full indexing, on a quarterly basis, of the Old Age Security pension and the Guaranteed Income Supplement.

Mr. Speaker, I was very disappointed during Question Period yesterday when some Members opposite hurled abuse at the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney).
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian people must wonder about the operation of this House. What they saw was an attention-seeking device designed to draw the attention of the medias to an individual.
Now, how much did this little game cost the taxpayers? The proceedings of the House were halted for over an hour, and yet Members opposite know that unparliamentary terms are out of order in this House. Who are the victims of such manipulation, Mr. Speaker? Our senior citizens, those people to whom we
owe so much respect and who are disappointed and disillusioned when they witness such goings-on.
The Members opposite keep on spreading uncertainty after bringing the country on the verge of bankruptcy. They allowed the country to live beyond its means and if we do not act now to cut the deficit, in a few years we will no longer be able to afford our social programs since the cheques will be returned by the bank marked "no sufficient funds".
On the subject of pensions, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister has said over and over again that no change will be made to the old age security pension before 1986. The GIS is fully indexed and the OAS is also indexed, but only when inflation exceeds 3 per cent.
Our Prime Minister has also undertaken to monitor the situation closely and even to make some changes before 1986, circumstances permitting. That is the truth, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: EFFECT OF EUROPEAN BEEF IMPORTS AND UNITED STATES LEVY ON PORK
EFFECT OF EUROPEAN BEEF IMPORTS AND UNITED STATES LEVY ON PORK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what is happening to agriculture in western Canada? The European Common Market is dumping its highly subsidized beef into Canada, and if New Zealand and Australia fill the quota allowed, plus that from the United States and Nicaragua, Canada will have even more imported beef this year than last year. Who loses? The beef producers of Canada do.
The United States Government is imposing a levy on Canadian pork entering its country, claiming that government subsidies in most provinces in Canada make it impossible for its hog producers to compete. Who loses? The hog producers of Canada do, including those in Alberta who suffer a double whammy. Albertans receive no government subsidy, and must also pay this levy, making it virtually impossible for hog producers in Alberta to compete or survive.
Grain producers are suffering from depressed prices, millions of grasshoppers, accumulated interest, and customs duties on farm equipment. Who loses? Our grain farmers do.
When our livestock producers and grain farmers go bankrupt, who loses? The consumer, who will then pay right through the nose for his food will lose.
A voluntary tripartite stabilization act, with no subsidization, and the payment of the Crow shortfall to producers in Canada, will help. Let us give our western Canadian farmers an opportunity to survive.

Mr. Speaker, the recently published report of the Commission of Inquiry on the pharmaceutical industry, headed by Commissioner Harry Eastman, made some valuable recommendations. Three important areas of investigation were as follows: first, the speeding up of the authorization processes for new drugs while ensuring their safety and efficacy; second, providing that compulsory licences ensure that licencees pay their fair share of research and development costs and that royalties are distributed in a way designed to encourage research in Canada; and, third,

providing more information to consumers on substitutability and prices.
All in all, Sir, the report gives authoritative directions for our pharmaceutical industry, and it is to be hoped that the recommendations will be implemented in a timely manner so as to ensure the availability of safe, effective, and reasonably priced drugs, to encourage research and development in Canada, and to increase the proportion of Canadian manufactured pharmaceuticals sold in our domestic market.

Mr. Speaker yesterday the Prime Minister and his Minister of Finance accused some of us on this side of the House of scare tactics. For the benefit of the Minister of Finance, Mr. Speaker, that means "non-sufficient funds".
Oh, oh!
I ask the Prime Minister: how is he going to restore that credibility?

Mr. Speaker, 1 was merely referring to what I think is an historical fact, that the deficits which began during the time my right hon. friend was Minister of Finance have led to a crushing burden-and I say this with no unfairness; I think it is a fact- which places in peril the capacity of the country to do that which we must do, namely, supply services to our elderly citizens. My question really relates to trust in government. The Prime Minister has broken a promise. At the same time that he broke his promise to our senior citizens his Minister of Finance was giving a $125,000 cash bonanza to everyone wealthy enough to have a capital gain. Will the Prime Minister keep his word, given in Sherbrooke last July? Will he restore his credibility and restore trust in government by restoring full indexation of senior citizens' pensions?
My right hon. friend refers to the two surpluses. His last two surpluses were in his first two Budgets, and the next two Budgets began the process of this country going belly-up.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR REASSURANCE OF ELDERLY ON PENSIONS ISSUE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, those Hon. Members do not like to hear that the debt of this country has been growing at 25 per cent per annum. That is three times faster than the country has been growing. You cannot go on like that forever. In 1979 interest on that debt was $8 billion; it is now $25 billion. That is now greater than what the federal Government is spending on medicare, Old Age Security and the Guaranteed Income Supplement. Mr. Speaker, before you, your successors or anyone else in the Chair make a ruling that could prove unfortunate ... It reads very well, and if there is something sacred in our British parliamentary system, it is the right to present a petition. What do you expect, if you are dealing with an issue, if a group of persons or an individual presents a petition it is quite proper that the names and object of the petition be made public, this is not a case where one simply says: I have a pile of petitions, here they are, thank you.
That is contrary to British parliamentary procedure, because the right to present a petition is a sacred right. Indeed it is quite clearly expressed: . . . who now exercise their ancient and unchallenged rights.
I rather doubt that anyone can give that right a definition which differs from what was intended, the right of the people to have their day in court. I would suggest that it cannot be done in a disorderly manner by saying: Here, Mr. Speaker, I have received a pile of petitions, I present them, thank you. I think people have that right, and since a basic principle might be established today I want us to reserve judgment on that.

The House resumed consideration of report stage of Bill C-26, an Act to amend the Old Age Security Act, as reported (without amendment) from the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs and on Motions Nos. 1 and 2 (Mr. Epp (Provencher)) (p. 6021).

Mr. Speaker, before the adjournment of the debate for Question Period at two o'clock, we were discussing Bill C-26. Our Party, of course, although we are in favour of the principles of the Bill-we are obviously in favour of anything which will increase benefits to people between the ages of 60 and 64-is of the view that the Bill could be much further enhanced if we were to remove the discriminatory clauses which make life so difficult for the 80,000 Canadians who will be discriminated against. I was about to describe to you at that time, Mr. Speaker, and I am sure you will recall it vividly, that single, separated and divorced people would be discriminated against.
Let me describe to you, Mr. Speaker, some of the difficulties we see. I was describing to the Chair before the adjournment that, for instance, in the case of a divorced person whose former spouse was perhaps contributing toward support and who subsequently died, that person would find herself in a similar condition to being a widow, because essentially she would be living alone with no other means of support than her own.
There is a further complication, Mr. Speaker. In some debates in the past I challenged this Government to arrive at a proper and equitable definition of a widow in terms of this Bill. Perhaps some Hon. Members of this House would say that "widow" or "widower" are both fairly easy to define because it means "one whose spouse has passed away". That is perhaps so, Mr. Speaker, but I would like to give you some instances where the Government could really get itself into a situation
Old Age Security Act
which would make it impossible to define who would be eligible for benefits and who would not. There is the case of a person who is widowed and will be receiving benefits. What about the case of a person who is widowed and then remarries? Of course, everyone will agree that that person is no longer a widow. But what happens to a person who is widowed, remarries and then divorces? Does that person go back to the original status of widow or widower? Will that person then be eligible for benefits?
There are numerous examples I could give to you, Mr. Speaker, and perhaps I will because I see you are insisting that I explain it further. I can describe to you just how these provisions are discriminatory and how the Government has got itself into a kind of situation, Mr. Speaker, which is totally unacceptable. The only legitimate thing to do is to expand those benefits, at least the one-year provision we described in the amendment. What we really want, and what we have been trying to convince the Government of for a long time through the presentation of petitions here today and on many other days, is that it should make benefits available to all needy people between the ages of 60 and 64. The "minister of social injustice", otherwise known as the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp), would surely understand that. In order to restore his proper title I am sure he will want to correct the provisions of this Bill which make the present legislation so discriminatory.
