speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
that the Bill be read the third time and passed.
He said: Mr. Speaker, Bill C-26, which has been in the House of Commons for some period of time, is a further effort by the Parliament of Canada to improve the benefits for Canadians in need of Old Age Security, specifically the spouses allowance. At the time this Bill was introduced I said I believed it would have the support of every Member of the House. During the discussion on the Bill there have been proposals, as recently as a few minutes ago, that it be extended to Canadians who are single, separated or divorced. We have looked at that very seriously and I guess there are two points which have to be made. The first is that those who say the legislation is discriminatory should be careful because, if that is the case, then one could make that charge against the spouse's allowance as well. If you discriminate against single people on the one hand, you could then discriminate against married people on the other, and I do not think we want to discriminate against either. It is my hope as the Minister of National Health and Welfare that over the life of this Parliament, as the economy improves, we can examine some of the proposals made by Members on both sides as well as those people who approached the committee regarding Bill C-26.
I think Members on all sides have had the experience of people coming into their office and explaining that they are unable to receive a pension by virtue of their marital status, that is, as widows they were not eligible for the pension their spouse would have received had he or she lived. What this Bill does is to extend to a group of needy Canadians a benefit for which they become eligible by reason of age and marital status. Therefore, Members of this House, and others who follow them, will no longer have to say to these people that they are not eligible for any benefit other than social assistance.
This legislation will affect approximately 85,000 Canadians, of whom it is estimated 72,000 are women. The legislation is targeted very specifically, not only to the most needy of that age group, but to women who are in greatest need. They have this need, frankly, because they have been homemakers and mothers for most of their lives. They have not been in the so-called workforce and have not contributed to society in a specific financial way. They are, after the death of a spouse, then faced with the prospect of having to go into the workforce, something which they have not done for many, many
years. As well, the work that is available to them, if it is available at all, is generally low-paid physical work which, by reason of age or health or both, they are incapable of performing. It is for those compelling reasons that the Bill was brought forward.
There is no question that we in government examined whether we could have gone further. I have said both here and in committee that the Government would like to move as far as it can on this pension issue, but we had to examine very carefully the financial realities. But despite restraint, despite the deficit and the costs it imposes on all Canadians, I believe the country is willing to move forward on this proposal on its merits.
We in this House hear a lot about pension reform. I am in favour of a very strong approach to pension reform. Those Canadians who are retired or close to retirement have limited flexibility in retirement planning, obviously. But those Canadians who are in the workforce or coming into the workforce have to recognize that planning for retirement is something that should be looked at much sooner than statistics indicate most Canadians do, that is in the last 10 years of their working life. If one starts thinking of it at the end, so to speak, and then starts to make plans, much of one's flexibility is lost. The House has a responsibility, and I have the mandate, for pension reform, not only incrementally as is being done through Bill C-26. I am not here to discuss the Budget right now. That is for another time.
You wouldn't dare.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Oh, no I would dare. The provisions in the Budget for the Pension Benefits Standards Act have been lauded by everyone. They provide the flexibility to enable people to plan for and develop a pension plan. The House must move further in that direction. The matter of a homemaker's pension and extended benefits under the Canada Pension Plan along the lines followed by the Quebec Pension Plan commend themselves to most Members of the House.
I do not look at pensions only in the narrow confines of the budget debate or the confines of Bill C-26, but rather realize that pension planning takes an entire lifetime. Our society must realize that it is necessary for Canadians to plan for retirement. I know that many people have had a limited amount of income which makes that very difficult to do, but we must educate young people just entering the workforce about retirement planning. I know that people do not like to think of that time in their life because they have other priorities, but they should not ignore the necessity of pension planning.
Our demography in Canada is changing. It is of very little value to argue the narrow issues of whether pensions are at the proper level or how many people are living in poverty. We must address the causes of poverty and what changes can be made by society in order to alleviate or reduce that problem. I am well aware of the number of elderly people living below the
June 20, 1985

poverty line. 1 do not think there is one Member of this House who would not wish to allocate more money to that segment of the population if it were possible. However, we must bear in mind the financial situation of the country. Government and society must address the issue of a population study.
The Green Paper on the Immigration Act dealt in part with the population future of Canada. At the present time, approximately 12 per cent of Canada's population is over the age of 65. It is projected that in 12 to 15 years that age group will make up between 18 and 20 per cent of our population. Therefore, we must become much more aggressive and cooperative in studying our health care system in order to provide proper health care. We must put a much greater emphasis on preventive health care and health promotion, because Canadians over the age of 65 access the health care system substantially more than the rest of society. It is necessary to realize that from the point of view of future planning.
We are in our first generation of health care. Public health care in Canada began in the Province of Saskatchewan and has evolved and developed for 25 years. That system is good as is their pension system. We must all realize that while the system is good, it must be adjusted to meet present realities. The House has the very distinct opportunity and responsibility to plan together for retirement income and the health care system. Other aspects obviously must be added. The Minister of Labour (Mr. McKnight) who is also the Minister responsible for CMHC, realizes that from the point of view of housing. There are various components which must be given much more emphasis, and that is what the Government and I intend to do.
In conclusion, I appreciate the support of Members of the House for Bill C-26. I believe it is a progressive and good step. Eighty-five thousand Canadians will receive approximately $600 a month for which they are not presently eligible. Of those, 85,000, 72,000 are women living in the most difficult circumstances. Those are the strong points which commend this Bill to the House. I appreciate the views put forward by Members in committee, which views have been noted by the Government. I appreciate the fact that all Members want to have this Bill passed. The passage of this Bill will enable us to put this program in place for September 1, 1985. I thank the House for supporting this Bill.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak on third reading of Bill C-26, and I can give the Minister the assurance that the Liberal Party, the Official Opposition, intends to support this Bill. However I believe that the point the Official Opposition has been trying to make is, that all the arguments mentioned by the Minister to justify granting the spouse's allowance to widows and widowers, and all the examples he gave his constituency office, apply equally to individuals who are single, separated or divorced.
Old Age Security Act
Mr. Speaker, it is true that this is just one step, but Bill C-26 must be followed as soon as possible by the next step.
Mr. Speaker, when this Bill is implemented, and when, starting September 1, and in the months thereafter, people come with their problems to our constituency offices, I hope the Minister and his Conservative colleagues will remember they were forewarned by the Official Opposition and the New Democratic Party.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words about the more general subject of pension reform the Minister referred to earlier. I think that if we really want to make any progress in this area and ensure that the next generation will have an adequate retirement income, we cannot afford to study the issue piecemeal, as was proposed in the Budget. We cannot afford the so-called bandaid approach.
I agree with the Minister of National Health and Welfare that young people must be persuaded to save money for a decent retirement, but how can we urge 1.5 million unemployed, how can we ask them to save money for their retirement when they do not have enough money to keep body and soul together?
I think that what the Minister said earlier about pension reform in connection with employment and housing is quite true. Unfortunately, the Government is doing the exact opposite. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) has made his own review of the situation. The Minister responsible for Housing makes his own decisions, and tomorrow he is going to announce closings and changes everywhere, without consulting a soul, and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) makes his own decisions again.
Mr. Speaker, the very important question arises: Can the private and public sectors absorb 1,400,000 unemployed? Can the private and public sectors respond to the Government's request to eliminate full unemployment? My answer is: no. What other means do we have to solve the unemployment problem and help solve problems for people who want to be able to retire?
Mr. Speaker, perhaps the parties and all intervenors, from all parts of the socio-economic sphere, should look at the broader rather than the sectorial aspects of the question. There are quite a few men and women who are now 59 or 60 years old and who are employed in the textile or footwear industry for instance, who work even if they are ill, and who are obliged to remain on the labour market for financial reasons. A large percentage of these people are not interested in going back to school to learn new technologies, and at the same time, we are telling young people who are trained: Stay home and collect unemployment insurance.
Mr. Speaker, I have an example of this in my riding, in the tobacco industry. This particular business had a surplus of 60 employees that it would have to lay off. Normally, according to the collective bargaining agreement, the last 60 hired would

June 20, 1985
Old Age Security Act
be laid off. The union and management agreed to offer early retirement to whoever was interested. The company did not rely on the Government alone, but offered all employees who were 55 and over and had a fair number of years of seniority, $30,000 in cash, in fact what the company calls its private pension. Mr. Speaker, to my astonishment, not 60 but 120 employees accepted the offer and applied for early retirement.
Because of this, not only was part of the productivity problem of this company resolved, but jobs were also created for younger workers because 120 people were offered the choise of retiring at 60 with a decent income.
For my part, I am convinced that if business, labour, the consumer groups and the Governments really got together, we could not only reduce unemployment, but also improve the income and the quality of life of people who wish to take early retirement. We had an example of early retirement programs in the shoe and textile industry because of plant shut-downs and designated zones. I am personally convinced that, as far as the unemployment insurance fund is concerned, if the Governments really wanted to do it, if we were to add all the money allocated to social programs, whether we are speaking about unemployment insurance, old age security or social welfare, all programs which obviously represent enormous amounts of money, which admittedly comes from the taxpayers and do not belong in the pockets of Members of Parliament, and including the social housing programs which are important to provide assisance to the needy because it is a fact that in certain places, there are two classes of poor people, namely the lucky ones who have the same old age security pension or welfare cheques as others, but who live in low rental housing, and the others who are not so lucky because, in Montreal, there is a waiting list of 1,500 people for this type of housing, and who, with the same income, namely the old age security pension or welfare cheques, have higher expenses because they did not have the good luck to find a low rental appartment

I believe, Mr. Speaker, that we must act urgently to allow people to take an earlier retirement, and I honestly believed that a new Government with 211 Members in Parliament had a marvelous chance to do something else than apply band-aid measures and that it would develop some real policies in this regard. In European countries where such things have existed for hundreds of years, retirement plans were not invented by Governments, but rather by unions and workers. The workers themselves manage the pension funds. Whether in France, Germany or somewhere else, pension plans were not invented by the Governments, but by the workers. The business managers who administer their own pension funds are the ones to decide how the money will be invested and they are the ones who tell the Government what should be the amount of the contributions and benefits. However, in Canada, while the Quebec Pension Plan works well in my opinion, we must be honest as far as the Canada Pension Plan, which applies to all the other provinces, is concerned. Everyone knows that any
surpluses in the fund are lent at preferential rates to the provinces. Politicians of all parties will have to stop putting their heads in the sand. The money contributed by all taxpayers to pay for a retirement fund will have to be invested to provide better returns than at the present time. It is no secret that the provincial Governments, except in Quebec, want an increase in contributions, but not in benefits. Why is it? Because they want a surplus in the fund which they will be able to borrow to build and pave roads. However, 1 think that we must have the political will to stop the Canada Pension Plan from being a means to finance or to assist the provinces, and this is one of the basic reasons for creating a real program for retired citizens.
Looking at the recommendations contained in the Budget, and even at those submitted by the Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs under the Liberal Government, some improvements are being made but still a large group of citizens in need are completely ignored. When one wishes to open the door to the private sector, which for years has had a chance to get into private sector retirement plans, there are thousands and thousands of employees in small businesses who for various reasons do not have private plans. And as long as we do not make sure that the Quebec Pension Plan and the Canada Pension Plan will provide a reasonable amount to allow for a budget with the basic Old Age Security pension, 1 do not think we will have solved the problem. People who will come here after us in 20, 30 years from now will be making the same speeches we are now making, and will still be doing patchwork.
Mr. Speaker, I will conclude on this. There is still reason to rejoice in the fact that, as of September 1st, 85,000 people will benefit from the spouse's allowance, but 1 will tell the Government it could have chosen to give something else to those people, instead of the spouse's allowance. Because it is indeed rather strange that one should get the spouse's allowance after having had no spouse for 20 years. This could have been the basic Old Age Security Pension that could have been made accessible, and as we know there is a difference dollarwise between the spouse's allowance and the basic pension. But even though I have been quite critical of the Minister, 1 must recognize that some commendation is deserved for helping 85,000 people. It is my hope that next year we will discuss helping 80,000 other persons, and the year after we will be doing the same for couples.

Mr. Speaker, 1 want to say a few words on third reading. Let me start off by picking up on what the Minister said about our pension and medicare system. He made reference to the fact that the Minister of Labour (Mr. McKnight), myself, the Hon. Member for The Battlefords-Meadow Lake (Mr. Gormley), and the Hon. Member for Saskatoon East (Mr. Hnatyshyn)
June 20, 1985

come from the Province of Saskatchewan where medicare first got its beginning. It actually started with hospitalization around 1946-47 around the time I was born. We had medicare in 1961 under Premiers Douglas and Lloyd. I think Saskatchewan led the way in social legislation and the kind of legislation we have before the House today. This kind of legislation is a positive step forward.
As we said before, there are a number of people who are discriminated against through no fault of their own who find themselves in poverty. I am referring to widows and widowers who are the ones, along with other pioneers who built this country, laid the foundation and made Canada what it is today. We as a younger generation ought to make sure that these people can live in dignity and have enough income in order to purchase the necessities in life. I support the measure before the House today.
We should keep in mind that about 42 per cent of the pensioners in Ontario, according to a recent study made public a few days ago, live in poverty. If 42 per cent in Ontario live in poverty, that percentage is surely a lot higher in Newfoundland, Manitoba and other provinces that are the so-called have-not provinces. We should be doing as much as possible to make sure that we extend to the seniors as many benefits as possible.
[ Translation]
As I said earlier, Mr. Speaker, we are all in agreement on Bill C-26 now before us. I would like to commend the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) for this measure. It will extend the spouse's allowance program to Canadian widows and widowers who are now in need, people between the ages of 60 and 64 who are now facing great difficulties in our society. As the Minister mentioned, there will be 85,000 people who will be helped by this measure, and they are mostly women.
But, Mr. Speaker, there is one thing I must say before this debate is concluded, and it is this: I support the legislation, as I said, but the Bill still is discriminatory. It discriminates against people who are single, people who are divorced, because under the Bill the spouse's allowance will be allowed to persons who are widows or widowers, but there will be nothing at all for those who did not marry or were divorced. And I wonder, Mr. Speaker, why such a discrimination? This is discrimination in our country and it is totally unfair, because we can find many examples of women or men who never married or who were divorced and now find themselves in the same economic and social situation as a neighbour who was married or whose spouse is now deceased, and then one neighbour will get the allowance while the other will not. In our society this is totally unfair.
As I said before dinner, we proclaimed the Charter in this country a few weeks ago-

We have the equality clause in the Charter of Rights. Here we are talking about equality on the basis of sex and every-
Old Age Security Act
thing else. Even though it is not in the Charter of Rights, this is an act of discrimination against single and divorced people.
In any case-

-I agree, we all agree on that, Mr. Speaker. Maybe we can all vote together for this legislation, and again 1 applaud the Minister of National Health and Welfare.

Mr. Speaker, there are just a couple of words that I want to say. I will not hold up the debate for very long. I think it is important to keep in mind that the measure before us today with its deficiencies cannot be held in isolation as far as assisting the needy is concerned. I wish the Government of Canada had a united front as far as assisting the poor and the needy is concerned. It is all well and good to say, "We are doing this as a positive measure to assist people with income", while at the same time you do not assist them very much when you increase fuel taxes. You do not assist them when you increase the sales tax and extend it. Those things affect the very people you are trying to assist in the legislation before us today.
All this has to be taken into account when one talks about a Government that is sensitive to poor people and people who need assistance. It does not help either, Mr. Speaker, to pretend sometimes that you are considering such and such a measure that will affect people adversely. Take, for example, the postal rate increase. That increase was approved ages ago by Cabinet. It is in effect now. Not very many Members know that. I have had that verified. Many things have to be kept in mind and you take them as a whole. Is the Government of Canada being fair and honest when it says it is being sensitive to the poor people, to the people who are affected by this legislation in the rural areas? They are the same people who were affected when the Minister in charge of housing, who was in the Chamber a moment ago, cut back on the home repair program. I say that because the new criteria for getting money for home repair mean, with the present cuts, that only people in certain economic circumstances who would benefit from this legislation can now take advantage of that program. To cut back on that program is not assisting those people at all.
We considered recently the end of the oil substitution program. The criteria for that affected the very people we are talking about today, the poor people. When you look at it all, it is done on the basis of a means test. A lot of the programs in CMHC under the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) are so directed. When Cabinet Ministers consider legislation such as this, they should think about their own Departments and how they can assist poor people. This is what the Minister of National Health and Welfare is attempting to do under this piece of legislation, although not completely. It is not good enough for poor people who are recipients of various government programs to have one Department that is trying to help and another Department, bringing in new regulations because of the Budget or the financial statement which dis-

June 20, 1985
Old Age Security Act
criminate against the same people, especially if the new regulations involve additional fees or charges.
I have another suggestion for the Minister of National Health and Welfare. A few moments ago he said that he was listening carefully to this debate and that he would see what he could do about some of the suggestions that had been made. In a previous debate I made a point about the fact that in the event of borderline cases, cases which have to be appealed or have to be decided upon by an independent board, all cheques emanating from the Department of National Health and Welfare or portions thereof are seized by provincial administrations because the individuals are on social assistance. If a person is really poor and is receiving social assistance, as is the case for many people affected by this legislation, the people about whom we are talking, this situation is not good enough. I could never understand how we got into that bind in the past. In fact, I cannot understand it today. I suppose it is because of good federal-provincial relations that when someone receiving social assistance suddenly becomes eligible for a federal pension or a payment from the Department of National Health and Welfare, the amount of money paid out by the provincial administration is taken 100 per cent from the federal payment, that is, the moment the person became eligible and throughout the appeal period. On the basis of the financial return to the federal Treasury, I hope the Minister agrees with me on the needs of the persons applying and qualifying for pensions but not receiving them because they are seized by provincial authorities with the agreement of the federal Department of National Health and Welfare.
I should like to put the example of a person receiving $8,000 before the Minister. That is a good figure to use because many of the appeals which go to the Minister's Department under its payment structure are around that figure. If that person has received $8,000 from the provincial Department of Social Services from the time he or she became eligible, and if he appeals through the Minister's Department, half of the $8,000 is paid from the federal Treasury in transfer payments under the Canada Assistance Plan. These payments are made at the end of every month. In effect, if $8,000 is paid out by a provincial Department of Social Services or Department of Welfare, $4,000 of it comes from the federal Government.
What happens after a person becomes qualified to receive cheques in the amount of $8,000 from the Department of National Health and Welfare? We must remember that a judgment had been reached prior to this point. Whether it is the Canada Pension Plan, a disability pension, an old age pension or a payment under the particular legislation before us today, a decision has been reached, the person qualifies, and what does the Government of Canada do? It passes $8,000 along to the provincial Government. How does it work? The provincial authority pays out $8,000, half of which is retrieved under the Canada Assistance Plan, so it actually paid out $4,000. Along comes the payment from the Department of National Health and Welfare which goes to the provincial
administration, and it ends up with $8,000 plus $4,000, for a total of $12,000 for paying out only $8,000.
I have tried to figure out how that is rationalized on the accounts at the end of the year. I still have not been able to do so. I cannot find anyone to tell me exactly how that amount is recovered. We are not talking about a large figure or about a great number of people, but we are talking about people in great need. According to my calculations, the provincial administration would stand to benefit $4,000 from that $8,000 pay-out.
I am sure the Minister of National Health and Welfare will check into the logic of what I have just said. He will find out that what I have said is correct. It has been going on for years. I am not accusing the Minister of implementing this when he took office. However, because of his good relations with provincial Tory Governments, the system of transferring money has become much easier since last September 4. In any event, he should check it out.
I would suggest that when someone is owed money by his Department, the Minister should pay 50 per cent of it to the provincial administration and the other 50 per cent to the recipient. Recipients believe that they are appealing pensions to which they are entitled. Therein the Minister of National Health and Welfare would be doing a great service for not all that many people, but for people who have been completely misled by the information which they received vis-a-vis their pension payments.
In conclusion, as I mentioned on another occasion, let us not forget that there are many people in the country who believe that when their pensions are increased or they suddenly become eligible for pensions, they will benefit in real terms. However, what about people on fixed incomes? We must remember that the amount of money a person receives depends upon the province in which he or she resides. I have never understood why provinces with some of the highest costs of living have the lowest payments. There are people between the ages of 60 and 65 today, with their children or grandchildren at home, who are receiving only the widow's allowance from the provincial Department of Social Services. Some provinces say that people 18 years of age and over who are able-bodied cannot receive any money under their social assistance schemes or do not qualify for family allowance payments. There are people operating under very tight budgets. We must keep in mind that many of them will not see any benefit at all because their social assistance payments will be removed. As well, people who are institutionalized and subsidized by this Government, directly or indirectly, only receive what is called the comforts allowance, whether it comes from social assistance, the federal cheque or wherever. As I said before, I have never been able to figure out why the comforts allowance in one province is higher than the comforts allowance in another province or why some of the richest provincial Governments- and Mr. Speaker knows the ones about which I am talking- have the lowest comforts allowance.

['My hon. friend, the government House Leader, observes that they just picked up the work that we were doing.
I do not think that that is an accurate statement. My clear recollection of the approach of the former Liberal Government was to ask lawyers to go over all the legislation to find what needed to be changed to comply with the Charter and to prepare amendments to do that. They were not asked to prepare discussion papers and to call these issues grey areas, but were asked to propose the amendments that ought to be made to bring the Charter into full effect in this country.
The time that I have spent with the subcommittee has given me some great insights into the real shortcomings of this piece of legislation. For example, I asked a lawyer who appeared before the committee what advice she thought the law officers of the Crown must have given the Government about changes that were needed. She said that she felt that the Government was in a sense hiding behind its grey area theory and was saying that more discussion was needed. 1 asked her for a concrete example of the sort of thing that the Government was calling a grey area but that would be patently obvious to any lawyer and indeed to any Canadian who would think about it that an amendment to a law of Canada would be required by the Charter. The example to which she referred was the rights of handicapped people to exercise their franchise.
Now, of course there is nothing in the law that prohibits the handicapped from voting, but what the Government knows very well is that the way polling booths are established on
June 20, 1985', 'voting day, absolutely no consideration is given to whether the handicapped can get into the polling station or not. Every Member of this House knows from his or her own experience that there are a great many polling stations into which handicapped people cannot enter. The lawyer to whom 1 spoke was confident, as I am, that this issue must have been brought to the attention of the Government and that some provision could have been brought forward to give the handicapped an option to vote in federal elections through mail-in ballots, as is done in a number of other countries, or perhaps at a polling station to which access is physically available. However, that does not appear in this legislation. I regret very much the fact that this is a technical Bill. I regret very much that the Government has taken that attitude toward the implementation of the provisions of the Charter.
1 would like to tell Hon. Members about something else I experienced while participating on the subcommittee that is looking into these so-called grey areas. Last night, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Nielsen) attended our meeting to explain to the subcommittee what he called the enthusiasm of the Department of National Defence for making equality a reality for women and others who have been closed out of full participation in the important work done by the Armed Forces.
The Minister showed mean-mindedness toward change. He told the committee that the Department was prepared to obey the law and to implement the provisions of the Charter. What he meant by that was that if, for example, the 10-year old girl who appeared before the subcommittee in Toronto the day before asking for the right which is now denied women to be a pilot could raise the support, could go to court, could win her case, could finance and appeal which would surely be forthcoming against a verdict that would be supportive of her, if the Department could examine the clause which gives it the right to override the Charter in certain limited circumstances, and if the Parliamentary Committee could not be persuaded to rubber-stamp the present arrangements of the Department of National Defence, then the regulations would be changed.
The Minister told us that there was a group examining various alternatives for increasing the participation of women in National Defence. He said that inquiries were being made of our NATO partners in order to find out what they were doing because God forbid that Canada should show a role of leadership in giving women equal rights in National Defence.
What the meeting last night boiled down to was that the Charter was not the impetus for the Minister of National Defence to put anything new on the table as far as women are concerned. He was telling us about recommendations that were made in 1971 by a Royal Commission which examined management practices within the Government. He showed us how much progress had been made in his Department since 1971, and I suppose that progress was made by the former Liberal Government, in implementing recommendations now 13 years old. However, would the Charter lead this Minister to do anything new? Absolutely not, and that is very regrettable.
Adjournment Motion
1 mentioned the Minister of National Defence specifically because he appeared before us last night. I think that any Canadian can see from this Bill that every Department of Government has acted in virtually the same manner. They have proposed technical amendments, bankruptcy law amendments and changes in language to conform to sexual equality, but regrettably progress in creating greater equality will not come from the Government. It will come from private citizens who will insist on their rights and will take the trouble to go to court and from those who, if defeated, can afford to appeal.
On the subject of appeal, the Governement has taken a pretty clear position, although there was some difference between the positions of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie), on whether or not Canada would be prepared on any basis whatsoever to assist Canadians in bringing cases to court to establish the meaning of the Charter. So far, the word on that is that no financial assistance will be given by the Government for the bringing of lawsuits to establish this type of right.
I conclude by indicating that Liberal Members will not obstruct this Bill. However, all of us regard it as a very great tragedy that an occasion that was looked forward to so much as being the moment when underprivileged groups would have their rights recognized is being deferred to the committee that is reviewing the document about grey areas and deferred to individuals who are determined and supportive enough to take their cases to court.
I want to close by expressing the optimism which 1 feel for the spirit which I detected in the Justice subcommittee. It is working with very great vigour and it is working extremely long hours. It is determined to travel to all parts of the country. However, the subcommittee cannot hear everyone who wants to be heard. Over 800 groups and individuals want to be heard. Obviously, the subcommittee would never be able to conclude its work and submit a report if it heard all of them. However, I think there is some basis for optimism that the subcommittee, even though it is dominated by government Members, may well make recommendations which will take us beyond the very limited and technical advances which have been made in Bill C-27.']

Mr. Speaker, I have had an opportunity both at second reading and in committee to make my representations with respect to this Bill. I believe that this Bill has the unanimous support of the House in terms of its content. There is one amendment on which I will say a few words and repeat an undertaking that I believe the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap) brought to the attention of the House, both at second reading and at committee, which resulted in a change to the Bill. I would like to also make one or two comments prior to doing that.
I think it is very important to understand that the purpose of this Bill is not to change policy. This Bill was brought in because lawyers in the Department of Justice thought that more than 55 Acts of Parliament as they stood would be viewed by courts as unconstitutional. As a result of that there were changes that were made, some of the changes being very significant.
In my view, and this is a personal impression, the powers with respect to search and seizure were long overdue, were absolutely necessary and as a result of a case that went to the Ontario Court of Appeal, the Southam case, we found that dramatically changed the search and seizure provisions which I think inure to the protection of individual rights. I certainly applaud this change in so many statutes. We even see statutes now with respect to the Income Tax Act where the powers of search and seizure have been dramatically circumscribed.
With respect to the question of the Immigration Act, which was the subject matter of the only amendment in the immigration Act, the Act as it read previously, Section 29(2) and Section 29(3) said this:
(2)	At the request or with the permission of the person with respect to whom an inquiry is to be held, an adjudicator shall allow any person to attend an inquiry if such attendance is not likely to impede the inquiry.
(3)	Except as provided in subsection (2), an inquiry by an adjudicator shall be held in camera.
There was no practical criticism with respect to the handling of this particular procedure prior to this Bill. The Hon. Member for Spadina brought up the point that as a result of the prospective amendment, which was Section 112, of the new Bill that what might happen with respect to this matter is that there could be circumstances under which a refugee might not

June 20, 1985
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms want to disclose publicly to some people who might be in attendance or to some newspaper reporters who might be there the circumstances under which he was claiming the status of refugee for fear that certain consequences might ensue. This might very well be not only to him, but to members of his family. It might be people behind the Iron Curtain, it might be people in Chile, it might be people in many other countries where the public circumstances would be of such a nature that great harm could occur to the family.
This is something that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Cros-bie), myself and all members of the Committee thought was a legitimate criticism and which prompted an amendment which I thought was satisfactory and which was agreed upon. That amendment is as follows: Section 112(3) now reads as a result of the amendment, Mr. Speaker, "except as provided in Subsection (2), an inquiry by an adjudicator shall be held in camera unless it is established to the satisfaction of the adjudicator on application by a member of the public that the conduct of the inquiry in public would not impede the inquiry and that the person with respect to whom the inquiry is to be held or any member of that person's family would not be adversely affected if the inquiry were to be held or conducted in public".
In addition to this particular amendment, there was an undertaking that representatives for the Department of Immigration and Employment and the Minister would closely monitor the actual workings of this amendment to ensure that no harm occurred in circumstances where potential refugees were making application for that status.
The Bill as a whole, and I have said this before, is a grat improvement because it puts in constitutional order many federal statutes that, with the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, might very well be held to be unconstitutional. It is no panacea. It is not the end of the process. Many Bills come before Parliament now that the Charter is here, where the Charter provisions have to be taken into consideration in terms of the due process. It is a start. It is a very, very substantial move forward. It is not the end of the line.
I hope that all Members of all Parties will believe that this is progress.

Mr. Speaker, this is not a substantial step forward in this Bill, but speaking for Her Majesty's Official Opposition, we are certainly not going to delay the movement of this Bill forward. It will have our support. What a great opportunity has been lost to Canada in this Bill to see some real progress in implementing the equality provisions of the Charter. What the Government spokesman- and I note the absence of the Minister who has taken little personal interest in the Bill from what I can see-the Parliamentary Secretary, who has followed the Bill and who I congratulate for his own personal dedication to moving the Bill forward to this point, indicated in his remarks really tells the whole story.
The story is that the lawyers in the Department of Justice thought that there were certain technical changes that ought to be made to bring some of the statutes into compliance with the requirements of the Charter. What has been lost is an opportunity to move ahead by implementing some of the significant provisions in the Charter which also require that the laws of Canada be changed.
I had the opportunity to spend a few days on the subcommittee of the Parliamentary Justice Committee. That subcommittee heard witnesses who told it about all of the things that have been left out of this Bill. They have been left out of the Bill because the Government considers them to be grey areas, as it said in its document on equality.
What has been done is just the technical minimum. There has mostly been changes in language like trying to find ways of making words that are usually of a masculine connotation not connote one sex or the other. Although 1 approve of that process, it does very little to advance the rights of women and of others for whom the Charter was brought forward and for whom there was a three-year waiting period that led to that great day on April 17 when the full provisions of the Charter came into effect. These people have found that the Government's approach toward implementing the Charter equality provisions is to make technical changes that have been recommended by lawyers.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (CANADIAN CHARTER OF RIGHTS AND FREEDOMS) AMENDMENT ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to speak on third reading of Bill C-27.
It was required three years ago that the Bill be adopted this spring. The three years were required to review all federal legislation in order to bring that legislation into line with the equality rights section of the Charter. It was thought that three years was time enough to cover a good deal of the legislation.
Unlike the previous speaker, the Hon. Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan), I am somewhat disappointed. In fact, my caucus colleagues, especially the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson), are disappointed at the small amount which has been done and the very narrow interpretation of the mandate by the Minister in drafting the Bill. He has taken a very legalistic approach. He has changed several words, but he has often fallen short of the intent of the original mandate. However, the changes which have been made, with one exception, are changes which we would not wish to oppose. Therefore, we will support the Bill.
I would like to reinforce what the previous Member said about the rights of the handicapped. Very strong committee work has been done during the last several years on the rights of the handicapped. It is a pity that the work which was done by that parliamentary committee was not reflected in this Bill. In the same way, generally, the rights of women are ignored. For example, rights of pregnant women were unfortunately denied in a Supreme Court case. A woman was discriminated against because she was pregnant, but the court held that she was not discriminated against because she was a woman. Men can make jokes about how men might be pregnant. The Mayor of Montreal lost his bet on that point. The fact is that something should have been done to correct the situation once the Supreme Court had pointed out that inequality in the law.
More generally, I find that there is an unsatisfactory tendency, which is reflected in the legislation, to treat the principle of equality in the wrong way. It is similar to the equality of the elephant and the mouse. The elephant is free to step on the mouse, and the mouse is free to step on the elephant. As a French writer suggested, the law in its majesty forbids rich and poor alike to sleep on park benches or to steal bread. That is not the intent of the Charter and of the people who supported the Charter in the matter of equality.
Equality must be not equality of strength, it must be equality of personal dignity. In other words, a weak person has the same personal dignity as a strong person. To set the rules in such a way that the strong can take advantage of the weak, is a denial of equality, not an affirmation of it.
I wish to speak on the amendment to which the Parliamentary Secretary spoke. I am glad the amendment was made, even though the Hon. Member for Burnaby voted against it in its final form. I would have voted against it had I been in his place. Nevertheless, we support the legislation as a whole. 1 appreciate that the Parliamentary Secretary outlined the amendment which was proposed originally, the objections which were made by myself and others, and the revised amendment as it appears before us. I also appreciate his reaffirmation of a commitment. As I understand it, it is a commitment to draw to the attention of immigration officials that it is our expectation that the rights of refugees will be sustained. A further commitment was made to monitor the operation of that clause to ensure that it does not fail, or, if it does fail, to ensure that action will be taken.
The amendment which was moved originally by the Hon. Member for Burnaby in committee, which, in its revised form, is now in the Bill, is something which we can live with on an experimental basis. It leaves the onus where it was in the original law, and where it should be. That is to say, a hearing at which a person makes his claim to refugee status will be held in camera unless some member of the public, journalist or other, can show that it would not hinder the progress of the hearing or endanger the claimant or his family to hold it in public. I regret that we have introduced that amount of uncertainty in a process in which a person's life or liberty, and the lives and liberties of other people, may be endangered in ways which neither a journalist nor other people concerned are likely to realize. I believe that the rights of the journalist should not take precedence over the rights of the refugee claimant. The penalty, if something went wrong for the refugee claimant, may be far greater than any possible penalty if something went wrong for the journalist. I regret that the Ontario Supreme Court decision was so quickly adopted by the Government and applied here. I am speaking, of course, of the Southam decision. However, the revision of the amendment in committee, and the assurances of the Parliamentary Secretary, help to reduce the risk and potential damage to refugees.
I wish to point out an anomaly. When the committee pulled Section 112 of the Immigration Act, it decided to make a move toward the application of the Charter. However, the committee did nothing else to remove certain kinds of inequal-
June 20, 1985

ity which exist in the Immigration Act. People who step off the plane at Pearson International Airport, Mirabel or anywhere else, who are regarded by the first officer whom they meet as possibly inadmissible are sent for examination by an immigration officer. He may send them to detention after which, when they go to an inquiry, they have the right of counsel.
At the point when they are sent for that first examination before an immigration officer, they are denied the right of counsel. Not the law, but the guidelines issued by the Executive Director of Immigration, forbids access to counsel, legal or otherwise. That refugee claimant, probably a stranger in the country, would hardly speak English-we don't get many refugees from English-speaking countries-although he or she might speak in a dialect which would be hard to understand. That person who does not know our laws is confronted with uniformed officers-perhaps he is on the run from uniformed officers in his own country-and he is denied the right of counsel at the point when he makes his first statement in front of an immigration officer.
That is unjust, Mr. Speaker. It is a denial of the right of counsel which our charter upholds for all people in Canada. This has been affirmed by the Supreme Court to the extent that it has maintained that a refugee claimant within our borders has the right to a judicial hearing with all that goes with it.
There are other inequalities which the committee overlooked in examining the Immigration Act. For example, a Canadian citizen who applies to sponsor a relative to immigrate into Canada, and whose appeal is denied by officials, has the right to appeal to the Immigration Appeal Board. However, a permanent Canadian resident, non-citizen, does not have that right. That is something which the Minister has addressed in legislation which she tabled yesterday. There are other problems with that legislation, but it is possible that if those problems are corrected it may be passed and adopted. Why is it not adopted in this Bill? Why is it not put forward when it is recognized that the courts will demand and require, if asked, that we give the same right to the permanent resident as is now enjoyed by a Canadian citizen?
With respect to the right of counsel, it is required in our Charter that everyone has the right to counsel when he is in danger of being deprived of life or liberty. Generally speaking, that means that if any of us are required to answer questions of any police force, we have the right to have counsel with us. People who are detained in an immigrant holding centre do not have that right.
Last fall, when the RCMP and CSIS separately interrogated people who were detained at the Avion Detention Centre near Pearson International Airport, these people were not given the right of counsel. We are told that the investigation by the RCMP and CSIS was necessary because they had to protect the Queen and the Pope from terrorists. Apparently no one told the RCMP or CSIS that the Queen and Pope had left the country several weeks before those interrogations took
Canadian Charier of Rights and Freedoms
place. Members of CSIS, by law, are allowed to read the newspapers, but apparently they do not, so these interrogations were held for reasons undisclosed and without the people being interrogated having the benefit of counsel.
Another point which concerns refugee claimants particularly is the right to work and to support themselves by their work. Some are given work permits, some are not. There are various circumstances and administrative decisions, but there is no law which supports their right to work. That is something which should have been considered in this Bill. The same applies to the right to schooling or medical care under our health insurance law. Our public schooling and public health services are not readily and certainly available to refugee claimants who have been admitted and who are awaiting determination of their status. That is a matter of equality, Mr. Speaker, which should have been addressed in this Bill and was not.
1 agree with those who say that the Bill is good as far as it goes. Except for a little uncertainty with respect to the treatment of in camera hearings for the refugee claimant, it is generally good, but it could and ought to have gone a good deal farther. When further consideration is given to this subject, as I hope it will be, it is quite important that people understand that "equality" means equality of human dignity and the protection of human dignity. That means the protection of the weak against the strong who can look out for themselves, rather than some mechanical and superficial bureaucratic approach which increases the power of the strong as against the weak. That principle has to be straightened out, Mr. Speaker, if we are going to make any serious progress in introducing equality into our statutes.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW (CANADIAN CHARTER OF RIGHTS AND FREEDOMS) AMENDMENT ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not my desire to prolong the debate on C-27 at this stage of the proceedings. I know there is an agreement to pass it in short order. However, I want to point out to the House that Bill C-27 is really one step in a process which, in the view of many parliamentarians, ought to be an ongoing process; that is the comparison of all Bills and legislative provisions brought before the House of Commons and the Senate to the provisions of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
When Parliament agreed to, and did pass, the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, it was clear that those provisions applied to all legislation passed by the Parliament of Canada. In order to pursue that legal position, there ought to be some ongoing method for examining legislative provisions to ensure compliance with the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. In fact, some steps have been taken to ensure that such a process is included in the procedures of Parliament, both in the House of Commons and in the other place, and that matter has been given consideration by the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and other Statutory Instruments.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for York Centre (Mr. Kaplan), as Chairman of that committee, and our other colleagues on the committee, have considered this matter and have recommended the passage of a resolution to the effect that all Bills be referred to the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and other Statutory Instruments for examination

June 20, 1985
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms to determine whether provisions of the Bill comply with the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Such a resolution was passed by the other place on February 26, 1985, and I think it ought to be considered by the House of Commons.
We realize that the same matter is under consideration as a result of recommendations of other parliamentary committees, particularly the Special Committee on Reform of the House of Commons, and all the recommendations might be brought together. We realize also that it would take time to review the situation to determine what exactly is the appropriate process to ensure that Bills and legislative provisions brought before the House of Commons are examined in this way to ensure compliance with the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

Mr. Speaker, there are grey areas in the Charter of Rights, especially concerning Section 15, and, to use a controversial euphemism, the matter has obviously been put off indefinitely or again referred to a committee for further study. 1 would simply like to share with the House a few opinions or points of view on minority groups, be they official languages minority groups or ethnic or linguistic minority groups. In my opinion, the House should know-
-that Section 15 does not preclude affirmative action programs. Many of us remain in the dark on the Government's position. We all agree that Bill C-27 is not the be-all and end-all of justice and equity; it does not radically change any laws. I think on second reading of this Bill I made a comment that a lot of the changes proposed were indeed semantical changes, words that were used to replace some other words.
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, the question which is of some concern to us and which I would like to share with the House relates to minorities who feel that their rights are being breached and would like to launch court appeals against certain sections of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. More particularly, I have in mind the Court Challenges Program which made it possible for certain minority groups-Anglophones in Quebec or Francophones outside Quebec-to obtain from the federal Government either financial or legal assistance to appeal against the implementation of a provision of the Charter.
Mr. Speaker, the House will recall that last April 30 marked the end of the Court Challenges Program administered by the Secretary of State (Mr. McLean). The Government has not yet deemed it advisable to re-establish this program. I often rose in the House to ask questions to find out what would happen to the program and I must say that I have not yet received a direct or satisfactory answer from the Government. They seem to be dragging their feet on this issue. They told us: Yes, the matter is under review, we will have an announcement to make in the near future.
I want to emphasize to the House that a financial and legal assistance program is important to official languages minorities. I say so because I think most Members of the House share that opinion. We believe that minority groups should be helped and supported by the majority. And we also believe that the federal Government is the agency and, perhaps, the level of Government most capable and best equipped to help minority groups defend and uphold their rights before the courts.
When I mention linguistic rights, I think in particular of certain groups from Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan or Alberta. I can say offhand that there are presently at least two cases in Alberta and one in Saskatchewan. We all know that the Government must or should take heed of the invitation from the Supreme Court regarding Manitoba.
Concerning this program of court challenges, in my view, the government has a duty to allocate funds and also human resources at the department concerned in order to help groups to have their rights recognized by the courts. If we have a Charter of Rights, Mr. Speaker, and if our minority groups, in order to assert, to clarify and to have their rights recognized, have to pay from their own pocket, then 1 believe a society such as ours, a society which views itself as open, generous and most of all understanding must put in place a program which is generous toward these groups who are eager to benefit from it, especially at the financial level. I know full well, for instance, having met recently with people from Alberta, that there is a case being heard in court about Section 23 of the Charter, concerning the schools. I also know of another case in the criminal courts, involving an individual wanting a trial in French.
It is essential, Mr. Speaker, that minority groups, and 1 refer to Manitoba, have the assurance within the next few days that such a program will be put in place, a program of financial assistance for court challenges, in order for these groups to get organized within the next weeks or months with a view to prepare their case to be submitted to the courts. They must have a well documented case so as to ensure good representation of the linguistic minority in Manitoba. I suggest that if the federal government and the Manitoba government accept the invitation made by the Supreme Court and

June 20, 1985
endeavour to present arguments concerning the delay for translation of the statutes of Manitoba which, as we know, have been declared invalid, yes, and ultra vires because of the fact they have been enacted in English only, then I believe that if we want to be fair toward the francophone minority in Manitoba, we must immediately assure them that a program will be available, providing money for court challenges. In this way, people will be able to claim from the federal government the assistance they need in order for them to have their rights recognized by the courts following this important decision by the Supreme Court.
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to delay the passage of the bill, but I would like the government to consider these problems that are viewed as important by all, that is human rights, the rights of Canadian citizens, and I would like the government to introduce within a few days in the Parliament of Canada this court challenges program. I know that all Hon. Members will recognize the importance of such a program which is valuable and indeed essential and which, I reiterate once again, Mr. Speaker, is urgent. It is absolutely essential that the government give us the assurance, thus eliminating any doubt, any concern we might have, that the federal government will step in to help minorities, be it in Manitoba, in Alberta, in Ontario or in Quebec or anywhere else in this country, in order for these minorities to have their rights recognized by the courts.
If I may hold the floor a few more moments, Mr. Speaker, I might add this: if the court challenges program is to be extended to include other provisions of the Charter, consideration might be given to including challenges to Section 15. I think that it would be a positive step that we on this side, would readily approve and heartily endorse. However, I repeat before concluding that it is extremely important to act without delay. We are asking the Government to make haste in this matter.

He said: Mr. Speaker, of all the aspects of this massive change to the Aeronautics Act, I suggest that this has probably been the most contentious. We have heard representations from a number of groups who were concerned first, with the initial wording in the Act, then concerned with the clause as amended.
It essentially involves a question of rights and obligations. It was my understanding that, according to the original clause, a private medical practitioner was required to have his patient, the holder of an aviation licence, to inform the Department of Transport of a medical condition within a specified period. Second, if this was not done, the medical practitioner would contact the Department of Transport.
As a result of discussions in the Transport Committee with a number of groups, and as a result of the circulation of draft wording by myself, with the assistance of the office of the Member for Regina East (Mr. Benjamin), the Government introduced an improved version of that clause. Quite frankly, when we sent to committee I was in agreement with the Government in its approach. However, as I listened to the witnesses and read material, I felt that we were making a fundamental error. We were removing the onus from the holder of that aviation licence to meet the requirements, particularly the medical requirements.
Therefore, we have before us an amendment which in effect amends my wording but changes the onus and puts it on the holder of the licence, whether it is a pilot or air traffic controller, where the onus belongs. The amendment states that the holder of an aviation licence must regularly report to a physician and an optometrist recognized by the Minister. Furthermore, that person must disclose to the medical examiner any medical consultations he has had in the past and
Aeronautics Act
indicate any medication he is taking. This will enable the Department of Transport physician to have all of the information he requires to make a technical evaluation of the capability of the individual to meet the requirements of the aviation licence.
Since the committee prepared its report we have heard representations again from the Canadian Owners and Pilots Association. Let me cite some of their comments with respect to Section 5.5:
We feel that we would be considered irresponsible and negligent if we failed to provide you, and the good members of your Committee, with the attached first-hand information as to how alarmed some knowledgeable and experienced physicians are over the subject matter. Dr. Bruce Lockhart, Dr. J. N. Armstrong, Dr. R. Webb and Dr. John Lockhart have all warned us that the present provisions of section 5.5 of Bill C-36 are contrary to the providing of a healthy atmosphere in which pilots may best perform their duties with utmost professionalism and care.
Furthermore, Dr. Webb wrote the following letter to COPA:
First, it has always been my understanding that every pilot is ultimately responsible for his aircraft and for his ability to fly it. This Act only serves to undermine this personal responsibility and place it in the hands of a Physician and of a Government bureaucracy.
A Physician already has too much paperwork initiated by third party requests which ask us to prove, in effect, that their client, our patient, is "not lying". We resent being placed in such a "big brother" position, which is what this legislation will do. If the medical problems being screened were of such significant frequency and importance, then * would not object, but where is the documentation to support such a Draconian measure? Although improvements can always be made, the current system already serves us well.
Second, and probably more important, this proposal will ultimately impede access to preventive health care for pilots. Pilots are only human and if their livelihood is threatened by reporting a health concern to their family physician, they are more likely to try and treat the problem themselves. For most medical complaints, this approach is not unreasonable, but for something more insidious and persistent, the results could be tragic.
For example, a recurring stomach pain/indigestion might imply a peptic ulcer to a pilot, who knows that he might be grounded if this was proven correct. However, left untreated, it might progress to a severe haemorrhage, with serious consequences for the patient, and increased costs for the taxpaper; or it could be even more sinister-a carcinoma!
1 would urge you to make every effort to have this portion of the Act altered. Pilots need encouragement to seek medical attention when necessary-not to be threatened by punitive legislation. Physicians do not want to be forced into a "spying" relationship with their pilot-patients.
Sincerely,
R. J. Webb, M.D.
Well, Mr. Speaker, we know the Government has good intentions in terms of how it has written this particular clause. The Government's intention must be to protect the travelling public as well as the crews, the pilots themselves, the air traffic controllers and also citizens at large who may be on flight paths. We heard of only one instance before the committee of a link between a medical problem and an accident. In that case, the Department of Transport know of the individual's medical condition and was unable to do anything about it. We cannot see on this side of the House how this forced reporting by the physician to the Department of Transport will change that. It certainly would not have changed it in the instance in Toronto.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when we were so graciously interrupted with respect to the due process of law enactment, I was replying to my colleague's comments and observations in support of his amendment.
As I was saying, the amendment presently before of us would have the effect of deleting any reporting requirement on the part of doctors and optometrists, which is proposed in the pertinent Section of the Act, Section 5.5, and substituting an obligation on pilots to submit to regular examinations by doctors and optometrists designated by the Minister and, during those examinations, to disclose details of all medical treatments or medications undergone since the last required or mandatory examination. The amendment also provides that the Minister may require pilots to undergo further medical tests or more frequent required examinations.
We suggest that this amendment would do very little to improve the existing situation, since the current legislation includes all the matters mentioned in the amendment by my hon. friend, except the compulsory optometric examinations and written reports to the Minister after age 40. Furthermore, the proposed amendment does not in fact address the issue that Section 5.5 was designed to answer, that is, how to make the Department aware of hazardous medical conditions. That principle lies at the root of this particular Section of the Act.
The Department, and I think all Canadians, are anxious that medical developments which occur between mandatory examinations in fact be reported. The small number of pilots who deliberately conceal dangerous medical conditions during required examinations is not so small as to make unimportant the provisions of the amendments before us to Bill C-36. As I said, only a small minority of pilots deliberately conceal medical conditions, but the effect of concealment on aviation safety can be tremendous. This problem has been recognized by the Department and by the medical profession itself.
In Ontario, coroners have found that undisclosed medical conditions were factors in at least four fatal accidents since 1978. In each case the coroner's jury recommended that there be some reporting mechanism available to all doctors who examine pilots and indeed holders of aviation documents.
In 1984 the Ontario Medical Association passed a resolution asking the federal Government to pass legislation authorizing doctors to report conditions on pilot patients that would make them unfit to fly and to protect doctors making such reports

June 20, 1985
from legal or disciplinary action. In fact, departmental doctors in every region of Canada receive calls each year from doctors inquiring wehther they will be protected from such action if they report a condition of a patient that makes his continuing to fly hazardous.
The provisions of Section 5(5) are similar to those found in the motor vehicle legislation of most provinces requiring doctors and optometrists to report conditions of patients that might affect their ability to operate a motor vehicle safely. In the case of motor vehicles, and even more so in the case of aircraft, the effects of an accident can be so serious to the public at large that the public interest requires that the usual principle of doctor/patient confidentiality be breached.
The section also makes it mandatory for a pilot to inform any doctor he consults that in fact he is a pilot. This is important because it may affect the choice of treatment prescribed by the doctor, since the chosen treatment may also have an effect on that same pilot's capacity and ability to safely fly an aircraft.
In short, I cannot accept the amendment as it fails to address the issues of providing a mechanism for doctors to make reports concerning conditions that may create safety hazards; protecting the reporting doctor from legal or disciplinary action and requiring the reporting of hazardous medical conditions that may arise between the required medical examinations.
Perhaps I should add, Mr. Speaker, that the report does not result in immediate licence withdrawal, or suspension. The only consequence will be that the pilot will be asked to undergo further medical examinations by departmental doctors. If the licence is withdrawn after these examinations the pilot will still have available to him the review procedures set out in the Bill itself. For those reasons we do not believe that we can accept the amendment.
However, I would like at this time, subject to your direction, to ask unanimous consent of the House for permission to introduce an amendment to the Bill. It addresses the concerns of the mover of the amendment in front of us, and goes some distance in dealing with part of the difficulties that we found with this.
The amendment I would introduce has to do with records, notices of decisions, application of certain provisions and a repeat of applications, limited by the fact that I would require unanimous consent to do that. I have had some consultations and I think the Chair would find an agreement to grant such unanimous consent.

Mr. Speaker, 1 want to thank the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary and his colleagues for accepting the principle that we put before them in committee, and in the notice which we tabled in the House quite some time ago. The amendment is to ensure that a lot of the so-called minor infractions that individuals may have on their records will be allowed to be removed, as long as they are not habitual in the sense that every six months or every year they are found to have not filed their papers on time, or other infractions.
I want to indicate briefly why we proposed the amendment. In doing that, I would like to give an example. We have had several representations from pilots, mechanics and engineers whose careers have been damaged because they did not cross a "t" or dot an "i".

June 20, 1985
Aeronautics Act
One example is that of the owner of a small engineering firm in northern Ontario. He has been a pilot for 15 years. In 1976 he was hired to ferry a small aircraft to another destination some 2.5 hours flight time away. He left with enough fuel for four hours, and was flying under normal conditions. However, two hours into the flight he had to make a forced landing because he was out of fuel. The landing was successful and there were no injuries. I would respectfully suggest that it was to his credit that he was able to do that.
He then received a letter from Ministry officials which alleged that he may have taken off without sufficient fuel for the trip. He advised them that the plane, which was owned by another individual, had a fuel pump problem and was pumping fuel overboard. No action was taken at that time. In 1981, he applied for his certificate of air worthiness for an aircraft which his company owned. The aircraft had not been in operation for some time. When he made his application, he forgot that that particular aircraft had a compulsory requirement to overhaul the propellers every five years. That period of time had elapsed a few days before he made his application to the CTA. His engineer's licence was suspended for 30 days for making an application for an aircraft which was not airworthy.
In the letter suspending him, he was told that the stiff penalty was necessary considering he may have taken off without enough fuel as a pilot almost five years earlier. This man's business came to a halt for 30 days. At that time his only recourse would be to the Federal Court of Canada. Through this amendment, at the very least, he will have an opportunity to have that record wiped clean. I say "opportunity" because clearly he will have to apply to the Minister and the Minister, according to this clause, has the right to say yes or no. If he says no, then the pilot will have an opportunity, as I understand, to take that to the appeal process.
I am pleased that we have once again been able to improve a very valuable Bill, to ensure that what passes this House is an effective instrument for doing what the Government, the Department and the industry wish it to do. I am pleased to have been a part of it and to have had this amendment accepted.
