Mr. Speaker, I want to make clear at the outset that this amendment, combined with the amendment we just passed, in effect deals with the period between the day that this Act is proclaimed and a point two years prior to that. It is the only time when, realistically, it is to apply. The intention is to allow those individuals who have been found guilty and have had a sanction or punishment placed upon them in the last two years to have access to the very valuable appeal system which has been established under this Act.
Until this Act passes, their only recourse is in effect to the same people who investigated them, who analyzed the situation and who decided on the appropriate punishment. What we want to do, Mr. Speaker, is to give them an opportunity to have that reviewed. I know that the Parliamentary Secretary will say that there are too many, that we will open the floodgates. While I recognize the number of infractions may be 700 or more over the last two-year period, clearly there are two groups.
There is the group which will feel that the infractions are of a minor nature and are not worth the time, effort and dollars to take the matter to the appeal process, things like failing to put in documentation on time-which was the case I read into the record earlier of missing the deadline for the propellor check. There is a second group however, which in that two-year period may feel they have been grievously wronged and we believe they should have the opportunity to present their case to the independent appeal tribunal. They should be given the opportunity to say they think a mistake was made, that justice has not been served either by their conviction or by the penalty in terms of their business, recreation, or whatever. 1 think very clearly we should give them that opportunity.
I understand there are regional variations in terms of the kinds of sanctions, depending on the investigating officers and the officials involved, so that one infraction in Atlantic Canada may be treated differently than the same infraction in western Canada. Because of that situation, as we perceive it, there needs to be that independent body to appeal to.
June 20, 1985

In the Enforcement Manual of the Department of Transport under the Table of Sanctions it states under Guidelines:
Although a purpose of the Table of Sanctions is to enhance consistency, the recommended sanctions are not hard and fast rules. Rather, they are suggested criteria from which deviations may be necessary according to the situation.
It is further stated, and I quote:
Mitigating circumstances are events that do not constitute a justification or excuse for the offence in question, but which in fairness, may be considered as extenuating or reducing the degree of moral culpability. Mitigation does not alter the fact of a violation nor does it provide a defence. It relates not to the offence but to the sanction. The sanction may be moderated in light of mitigation.
They list the mitigating circumstances as: lack of intent, misunderstanding or misconception and honest mistake. And under "aggravating circumstances" which is a severe category, it states:
Aggravating circumstances are events that show a significant degree of moral culpability in the violation. Examples are:
(i)	deliberate actions done with intent to commit a violation;
(ii)	negligence;
(iii)	Recklessness; or,
(iv)	habitual non-compliance shown by a series of recurrent violations.
When one compares the mitigating circumstances and the aggravating circumstances, one sees some similarities. A misunderstanding or a misconception could result in negligence. Which shall it be? An honest mistake may lead to recklessness. The point I am trying to make is that if we do not give those people who have been found guilty of an infraction over the past two years that option to go through an appeal, they are lost for at least two years. Clearly, they can wait for two years to decide to apply to have their record cleansed, but 1 do not think that we should set them aside as a separate category. I believe we should allow them access to justice. We should give them that opportunity, should they so desire, to appear before an appeal tribunal and state their case. The Ministry could then state its case and the tribunal could say yes, we agree, or no, we do not, or you are guilty but the treatment was too harsh.

Take the case of, say, a mechanic working for an airline in northern Quebec who replaced a fuel pump on a Cessna 172. The fuel pump he used had more hours on it than allowed for the type of aircraft he was working on. However, it could have been used for another 400 hours in several other aircraft before it had to be replaced. He simply made an error in the type of aircraft he put it in. No failure occurred. Certainly there was no malice on his part. However, the Government suspended his licence for two weeks. Not only did he not have an income for that period of time, the fact he has a suspension on his record has caused problems in advancing his career and his present employers worry about having him as a mechanic in the future for fear there might be another mistake.
Surely that is the kind of situation where the person involved should not have to wait another two years. He should be able to go to a tribunal and present his case. In this particular case, it seems to me, he deserves the right to have his case reviewed without the expense of going to Federal Court, but without this amendment he cannot do that. He can only wait for another two years or go to the expense of applying to Federal Court.
Surely there must be dozens of instances like that. Under this new legislation, once it is proclaimed, the person concerned will be able to start with a clean slate. His record is clear. subtopic: HEALTH-NATIONAL EPIDEMIOLOGICAL CENTRE PROPOSAL. (B) MONITORING OF BIRTH DEFECTS
HEALTH-NATIONAL EPIDEMIOLOGICAL CENTRE PROPOSAL. (B) MONITORING OF BIRTH DEFECTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 23, 1985, I raised a question with the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) regarding the funding for research in this country as it relates to the tracking, primarily of birth defects, but illnesses in general. I was referring to the Canadian Congenital Anomalies Surveillance System, and concerns raised about the lack of proper funding to do the kind of job that must be done in order to monitor birth defects.
My interest in the question stems from personal knowledge of situations, as well as an awareness of what is happening to our environment. While we know that particular forms of wildlife and plant life are indicators, or barometers, of the impact of man's treatment of the environment, we must also recognize that the human body is also a barometer. Unfortunately, some of those indicators show as defects in new born children. We see throughout the land what are called "hot spots". These are areas of the country where a particular defect in human beings is above average, whether it is congenital heart defects, missing limbs or other defects. There are hot spots out there and they are beginning to become documented.
It is my position that we should do what we can do to ensure that the necessary funds are available to continually track those defects that result from what we do to the environment but cannot see. For example, there are the effects of PCBs and radiation or lead poisoning that we cannot see immediately. One's arm does not drop off or one's skin does not change colour from low levels of radiation. However, in the long term, they may have some impact.
One method for sending a warning signal is by tracking birth defects. For example, there is very sound evidence of effects on unborn children as a result of mothers who smoke or consume alcohol. We warn expectant mothers to stay away
from radiation from video display terminals. However, do we warn them to stay away from an area like Serpent River in Elliot Lake where the mine tailings were flowing into the river? What was the effect of that radiation on the young men and women who lived at Quirke Mine site, north of Elliot Lake, right beside the Serpent River? Do they have children today who are not completely formed or did they have children who did not live to see today?
I believe the time has come to put our efforts into this early warning system. While we may not be able to help those young children who are the evidence of the effects of what we have done to our environment, we should be able to use it to discover what caused this problem so that we can make changes in our laws that govern how we handle substances that have an effect on the human body.
We may find that man had nothing to do with these effects but that a natural phenomenon caused the high incidents of a particular abnormality. However, we have a responsibility to society to research this as much as we can. One technique is through full epidemiological analysis of births in this country.
I would like to see us go even farther than that and have a system in Canada that would compile information on diseases, on illnesses, on defects and put all of that in one computer with automatic sharing of information with the provinces and municipalities. It should include death records where there are high incidences of death from specific illness in certain communities.
We have to remember that something happening today does not impact tomorrow. The folks in Kenora who are worried about the PCB spill will not know for 20 years, for all intents and purposes, if that spill has had any effect on them. We need that kind of tracking system so we can work backwards and find out where the common element is.
Let me come back to Quirk mine site at Elliot Lake. Where are all the young people and the adults who worked in the Ontario Ministry of Corrections Institute today? We should track them. Let us find out what has happened to them. Is there an above normal incidence of birth defects in their offspring? We will never know the answers until we begin to track situations. That is why on April 23 I asked the Minister to consider this question. I note that he indicated at his Health Minister's meeting on May 16 and 17 that they would look to the future together. Perhaps the Parliamentary Secretary can respond and tell us that the Ministers have looked at the question and will be providing the funding necessary for such a program.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre H. Vincent (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Revenue and Canada Post):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
subtopic: HEALTH-NATIONAL EPIDEMIOLOGICAL CENTRE PROPOSAL. (B) MONITORING OF BIRTH DEFECTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the accidental PCB spill in Northwestern Ontario has created renewed interest in the immediate and long term effects of environmental contamination. For this reason, questions have been raised in this House regarding the federal of monitoring
June 20, 1985

programs and their role both in the detection of high occurrence diseases and the study of their causes. I would like to describe the goals and expectations of the monitoring program and clarify the Government's position as regards environmental diseases.
Health monitoring has been defined as a thorough and onging review of all the aspects of the outbreak and dissemination of a disease that are useful to the implementation of effective control measures. The word "control" therefore involves the collection and systematic and ongoing assessment of a whole range of data on health and the communication of information to all parties that take part in control efforts. A surveillance system serves two main purposes. First, it must help assess the various health risks and provide an opportunity to use information gathered to design specific programs to fight diseases or to adjust existing programs to new conditions. Second, it must help establish differences between various population groups as far as the risk they run to contract a disease is concerned and thus facilitate the gathering of essential information on the thrust to give to such programs as well as provide for the assessment of action which has been taken.
Without minimizing the Government's concern over the recent PCB spill, it should be clear that this type of accident is not a surveillance issue in the usual sense. In fact, no practi-
Adjournment Debate
cable disease surveillance program could be expected to detect health effects such as cancer or birth defects from such a spill. The timing, location and extent of the contamination is known, as is the toxicology for short-term health effects. Persons who may have been exposed can be medically evaluated and have their health status checked periodically.

Guidelines on the transport of hazardous chemicals are being strengthened. Also there have been new regulations under the Environmental Contaminants Act which govern the disposal of waste oils containing PCBs. The Department of National Health and Welfare is working with its provincial counterparts and is seeking their participation in an enhanced sharing of provincial health data and federal disease surveillance services. This type of federal-provincial co-operation is required to increase the sensitivity and efficiency of our current disease surveillance systems. In this way, we will be able to further refine out surveillance abilities.
